A.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of vascular pathologies
A.q: Where does deep vein thrombosis rank among cardiovascular causes of death?
opts: Third most common

Correct. Deep vein thrombosis, a clot in a deep vein typically in the legs, is the third most common cause of death from cardiovascular diseases, so the venous side is not the minor partner it might appear.
First most common
It ranks third among cardiovascular causes of death rather than first.
Tenth most common
Its rank is considerably higher than tenth, at third among cardiovascular causes of death.
It is not a significant cause of death
It is the third most common cause of death from cardiovascular disease.
A.cite: SV Vascular Pathophys I Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 37

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of different pulmonary diseases, including: Restrictive pulmonary diseases
A.q: How does nephrotic syndrome cause a pleural effusion?
opts: It raises vascular hydrostatic pressure
Raised hydrostatic pressure is the heart failure and portal hypertension route.
It lowers pleural space pressure
Decreased pleural space pressure follows lung collapse; nephrotic syndrome acts through oncotic pressure.
It inflames the pleural membrane
Inflamed, permeable pleura produces an exudate; nephrotic syndrome produces a transudate.
It lowers plasma oncotic pressure
Correct. Decreased plasma oncotic pressure, from severe hypoalbuminemia, nephrotic syndrome (protein loss) or cirrhosis (less albumin synthesis), lets fluid collect in the pleural space.
A.cite: 9. Pulmonary Pathophysiology - Ward 2026 (rebuilt from recording).pptx, Slides 93, 94

A.io: Describe the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of coagulation disorders
A.q: What does von Willebrand factor do?
opts: Activates factor X together with factor IXa
Activating factor X is the job of IXa with its cofactor VIIIa. Von Willebrand factor supports platelet adhesion and carries and stabilizes factor VIII.
Degrades fibrin once a clot has formed
Degrading fibrin is plasmin's job in fibrinolysis. Von Willebrand factor supports platelet adhesion and carries and stabilizes factor VIII.
Supports platelet adhesion and stabilizes factor VIII
Correct. Von Willebrand factor supports platelet adhesion and carries and stabilizes factor VIII, which is why von Willebrand disease is listed with the hemophilias as a bleeding disorder.
Limits coagulation together with protein S
Activated protein C with protein S (and antithrombin) limits coagulation. Von Willebrand factor supports platelet adhesion and stabilizes factor VIII.
A.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 46

A.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of vascular pathologies
A.q: What are the two main pathogenic mechanisms of vasculitis?
opts: Immune-mediated inflammation, and pathogen invasion
Correct, and the distinction matters because the wall is being destroyed in one case by the host's own response and in the other by the organism itself.
Lipid accumulation and calcification
Those are steps in atherosclerosis rather than vasculitis mechanisms.
Mechanical stress and loss of elastic tissue
Those underlie hypertensive vessel change and aneurysm formation.
Valve insufficiency and venous stasis
Those belong to the venous side, producing varicosities and thrombosis.
A.cite: SV Vascular Pathophys I Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 32

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of valvular stenosis, regurgitation, and prolapse
A.q: What is a vegetation?
opts: A calcified nodule on the valve annulus
Vegetations are organisms within fibrin rather than calcific nodules.
Microorganisms enmeshed in fibrin deposits
Correct. As they enlarge they interfere with valve function and predispose to embolism, so the lesion does harm in two distinct ways.
A ballooned segment of valve leaflet
That describes prolapse. A vegetation is microorganisms enmeshed in fibrin deposits on the valve.
A thrombus within the left atrial appendage
Atrial clot relates to atrial fibrillation in mitral stenosis.
A.cite: 6. Cardiac Pathophysiology for posting.pptx, Slide 56

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of different pulmonary diseases, including: Pulmonary malignancies
A.q: Why is squamous cell carcinoma of the lung often detected earlier than other lung cancers?
opts: Sputum cytology can show it
Correct. Two-thirds arise in the central bronchi near the hilus as intraluminal growth, so sputum cytology shows the cancer and detection comes earlier.
It doubles in about 33 days
Rapid doubling in about 33 days is small cell carcinoma, and speed does not make detection earlier.
It arises in the lung periphery
Peripheral growth is adenocarcinoma, which is NOT as amenable to early detection.
Its large cells form visible nests
Large cells in nests or clusters describe large cell carcinoma, which also develops peripherally.
A.cite: 9. Pulmonary Pathophysiology - Ward 2026 (rebuilt from recording).pptx, Slides 25, 26, 27

A.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of blood disorders
A.q: What is the cause of factor V Leiden thrombophilia?
opts: An autoimmune response
An autoimmune response causes antiphospholipid syndrome, the other thrombophilia. Factor V Leiden is a genetic mutation.
A factor V deficiency
Factor V Leiden causes excessive clotting, not the bleeding a deficiency would; the bleeding deficiencies listed are factor VIII and IX (hemophilia A and B). Its cause is a genetic mutation.
An immune reaction to heparin
An immune reaction to heparin is heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, a platelet disorder. Factor V Leiden is a genetic mutation.
A genetic mutation
Correct. Factor V Leiden is a thrombophilia (excessive clotting) caused by a genetic mutation; antiphospholipid syndrome, the other thrombophilia listed, is an autoimmune response.
A.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 46

A.io: Describe the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of coagulation disorders
A.q: Which pair converts prothrombin to thrombin?
opts: Factor IXa with factor VIIIa
IXa with VIIIa is the step BEFORE: it activates factor X. Prothrombin is converted to thrombin by Xa with Va.
Tissue factor with factor VIIa
Tissue factor-VIIa starts the sequence by activating IX and X. Prothrombin is converted to thrombin by Xa with Va.
Factor Xa with factor Va
Correct. In thrombin generation, Xa with its cofactor Va converts prothrombin (II) to thrombin (IIa); thrombin then turns fibrinogen (I) into fibrin.
Factor XIIIa with fibrin
XIIIa acts on fibrin at the very end, producing crosslinked fibrin. Prothrombin is converted to thrombin by Xa with Va.
A.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slides 43, 44

A.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms involved in immune processes
A.q: How does interstitial fluid enter a lymphatic capillary?
opts: Through smooth muscle pores in the wall
Fluid does not pass through pores in a muscle layer; it enters between overlapping endothelial cells, whose edges open like one-way valves.
By active pumping across a basement membrane
No pump moves fluid in. Interstitial fluid flows in passively where the overlapping endothelial edges part, which work like one-way valves.
Between overlapping endothelial cells
Correct. The capillary wall is built of overlapping endothelial cells whose edges act as valves: they open to let interstitial fluid in and close behind it, so flow runs one way.
Driven in by the heart's systolic pressure
The heart does not drive lymph. Fluid enters between overlapping endothelial cells, and outside forces such as muscle movement keep lymph moving.
A.cite: Immunity_Lecture_Recorded.pptx, Slide 7

A.io: Describe the function of the complement system
A.q: Which components assemble the membrane attack complex?
opts: C1 with C4 and C2
C1, C4 and C2 begin the classical pathway, far upstream of the attack complex.
C3a and C5a
C3a and C5a are released fragments that promote inflammation.
Factor B and factor D
Factor B and factor D act in the alternative pathway to form a C3 convertase.
C5b with C6–C9
Correct. C5b initiates assembly of the terminal components C6–C9, and the assembled complex forms pores in a susceptible target membrane.
A.cite: Immunity_Lecture_Recorded.pptx, Slides 68, 71

A.io: Discuss the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of red blood cell disorders
A.q: What does anemia reduce?
opts: The blood's plasma volume
Anemia is a fall in hemoglobin, not in plasma; a reduced plasma volume with normal red-cell mass is relative erythrocytosis. Anemia reduces oxygen-carrying capacity.
The blood's clotting factor supply
Clotting factors belong to the plasma and the coagulation reactions. Anemia reduces the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity.
The marrow's white-cell output
Suppressed white-cell production is part of leukemic cytopenias, not the meaning of anemia. Anemia reduces the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity.
The blood's oxygen-carrying capacity
Correct. Anemia reduces the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity, which is why it is defined by hemoglobin below the cutoff for age, sex and pregnancy status.
A.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 35

A.io: Compare and contrast the functions of the various types of antibodies and the various mechanisms by which antibodies destroy antigens
A.q: Which immunoglobulin crosses the placenta?
opts: IgM
IgM is usually secreted as a pentamer and is often the first class in a new response; it does not cross the placenta.
IgG
Correct. IgG crosses the placenta and provides maternal protection; it is also the most abundant serum class.
IgA
IgA protects mucosal surfaces and reaches the infant in breast milk, not across the placenta.
IgE
IgE binds mast cells and basophils in allergy and parasite defense.
A.cite: Immunity_Lecture_Recorded.pptx, Slides 44, 46

A.io: Explain the pathophysiology of cardiac ischemia
A.q: Which determinants of workload increase myocardial oxygen demand?
opts: Coronary perfusion pressure and collateral circulation
These are supply-side factors rather than determinants of demand.
Heart rate, preload, afterload and contractility
Correct. Raising any one of the four raises demand, which is why ischemia can appear with the coronary anatomy entirely unchanged.
Plaque size and composition
These affect supply rather than the work the heart is doing.
Serum lipoprotein concentration
Lipoproteins relate to plaque formation rather than to moment-to-moment oxygen demand.
A.cite: 6. Cardiac Pathophysiology for posting.pptx, Slide 31

A.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of pulmonary pathologies
A.q: What does alpha-1 antitrypsin normally do in the lung?
opts: Secretes surfactant into the alveoli
Surfactant is secreted by type II pneumocytes; alpha-1 antitrypsin is a protective antiprotease enzyme.
Releases proteases from neutrophils
Proteases from neutrophils and macrophages DESTROY alveoli; alpha-1 antitrypsin opposes them.
Inhibits breakdown of alveolar tissue
Correct. Alpha-1 antitrypsin is a protective enzyme that inhibits proteolytic breakdown of alveolar tissue; its hereditary deficiency causes about 1% of emphysema.
Clears mucus from the bronchi
Mucus clearance is the work of the ciliated epithelium (mucociliary clearance).
A.cite: 9. Pulmonary Pathophysiology - Ward 2026 (rebuilt from recording).pptx, Slides 53, 54

A.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of vascular pathologies
A.q: What characterizes a saccular cerebral aneurysm?
opts: Uniform dilation of the entire vessel circumference
That is a fusiform aneurysm, in which atherosclerosis may be a factor.
A lesion arising from infected emboli
That is a mycotic aneurysm, usually in the setting of infective endocarditis.
A blood-filled channel within the wall layers
A blood-filled channel within the wall layers is a dissection rather than a localized dilation.
A thin-walled protrusion lacking elastic lamina

Correct, with very thin or absent tunica media. The lack of elastic lamina is named as the MAIN feature, and these are typically acquired rather than congenital. The tunica media is very thin or absent.
A.cite: SV Vascular Pathophys I Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 30

A.io: Compare and contrast the morphology of the various types of antibodies
A.q: Approximately what share of serum immunoglobulin is IgG?
opts: Less than 1%
Less than 1% is the share of IgD and of IgE; IgG is the most abundant class, at 75–80%.
5–10% is the approximate share of IgM; IgG makes up about 75–80% of serum immunoglobulin.
10–15% is the approximate share of IgA; IgG makes up about 75–80% of serum immunoglobulin.
Correct. IgG is the most abundant class, approximately 75–80% of serum immunoglobulin (700–1700 mg/dL); reference intervals vary by laboratory.
A.cite: Immunity_Lecture_Recorded.pptx, Slide 46

A.io: Review the anatomy of the blood cells
A.q: Where do T-cell precursors develop?
opts: Bone marrow
The bone marrow is where the B-cell precursor develops. T-cell precursors develop in the thymus.
Germinal centers
Germinal centers are where activated B cells undergo somatic hypermutation and affinity maturation. T-cell precursors develop in the thymus.
Thymus
Correct. The lymphoid progenitor branches into the B-cell precursor in the bone marrow and the T-cell precursor in the thymus, the origin of T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma.
Spleen
The spleen is not where T-cell precursors develop. The lymphoid progenitor branches into the B-cell precursor in the bone marrow and the T-cell precursor in the thymus.
A.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 24

A.io: Discuss the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of red blood cell disorders
A.q: Which condition can blunt the reticulocyte response to hemolysis?
opts: Renal disease

Correct. With hemolysis, erythropoietin and reticulocyte production usually rise when the marrow can compensate, but the response may be inadequate with marrow disease, nutrient deficiency, renal disease or infection.
Rising erythropoietin

Erythropoietin usually INCREASES when the marrow can compensate for hemolysis, and it drives reticulocyte production up rather than blunting it. Renal disease is one of the conditions that can make the response inadequate.
Recovery from anemia
Recovery from anemia is not among the conditions that blunt the response to hemolysis. Marrow disease, nutrient deficiency, renal disease or infection can make the reticulocyte response inadequate.
Dehydration
Dehydration reduces plasma volume and raises the hematocrit (relative erythrocytosis); it is not listed as blunting the marrow. Renal disease is.
A.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 37

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of different pulmonary diseases, including: Acute respiratory failure
A.q: Myasthenia gravis causes acute respiratory failure through which category of cause?
opts: Central nervous system
Central nervous system causes are sedatives, stroke and brain trauma or tumor.
Chest skeletal system
Chest skeletal causes are kyphoscoliosis, chest trauma, pleural effusion and massive ascites.
Neuromuscular disease
Correct. Neuromuscular causes are multiple sclerosis, myasthenia gravis, polio, Guillain-Barré syndrome and quadriplegia.
Pulmonary parenchyma
Parenchymal causes are shock, pulmonary embolism, pulmonary edema, advanced emphysema, pneumonia and acute respiratory distress syndrome.
A.cite: 9. Pulmonary Pathophysiology - Ward 2026 (rebuilt from recording).pptx, Slide 14

A.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of vascular pathologies
A.q: What are the final two steps of the atherosclerotic sequence?
opts: Monocyte adhesion, then platelet adhesion
Monocyte and platelet adhesion are early steps, following lipoprotein accumulation rather than closing the sequence.
Lipid accumulation, then calcification

Correct. After smooth muscle proliferation, matrix production and T cell recruitment, the sequence closes with lipid accumulation and then calcification of the extracellular matrix and necrotic debris.
Endothelial injury, then lipoprotein accumulation
Endothelial injury and lipoprotein accumulation are the first two steps rather than the last two.
T cell recruitment, then smooth muscle migration
Smooth muscle recruitment precedes T cell involvement, and both come before lipid accumulation and calcification.
A.cite: SV Vascular Pathophys I Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 25

A.io: Describe the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of myeloproliferative syndromes
A.q: Which disorder is one of the myeloproliferative neoplasms?
opts: Immune thrombocytopenia

Immune thrombocytopenia is not among the myeloproliferative neoplasms, which are chronic myeloid leukemia, polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia and primary myelofibrosis. Watch the ending: thrombocythemia, not thrombocytopenia.
Essential thrombocythemia
Correct. The myeloproliferative neoplasms are chronic myeloid leukemia, polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia and primary myelofibrosis: clonal proliferations of myeloid cells.
Chronic lymphocytic leukemia

Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is a mature B-cell neoplasm, a lymphoid disease. The myeloproliferative neoplasms are myeloid: chronic myeloid leukemia, polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia, primary myelofibrosis.
Hereditary spherocytosis

Hereditary spherocytosis is not among the myeloproliferative neoplasms (chronic myeloid leukemia, polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia, primary myelofibrosis). Essential thrombocythemia is the one listed here.
A.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 18

A.io: Compare and contrast the functions of the various types of antibodies and the various mechanisms by which antibodies destroy antigens
A.q: What is opsonization?
opts: Coating that eases ingestion by phagocytes
Correct. In opsonization antibody joins antigen on the cell's surface, and this coating facilitates ingestion of the antigen by a phagocyte.
Clumping of particles into a lattice
Clumping particles together is agglutination; opsonization coats a target so a phagocyte ingests it.
Pore formation in a target membrane
Pore formation is the complement membrane attack complex leading to lysis.
Blocking a toxin from its target
Blocking a toxin's action is neutralization; opsonization is a coating that eases phagocyte ingestion.
A.cite: Immunity_Lecture_Recorded.pptx, Slide 55

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of white blood cell disorders
A.q: Which three causes should a raised eosinophil count bring to mind first?
opts: Chronic infections such as tuberculosis
Chronic infections such as cytomegalovirus and tuberculosis are listed for a raised MONOCYTE count. For eosinophils the three first thoughts are allergy, parasites and drug effects.
Acute bacterial inflammation and sepsis
Acute bacterial inflammation goes with neutrophilia, and a band rise with infection. A raised eosinophil count points first to allergy, parasites or a drug effect.
Allergy, parasites and drug effects
Correct. Think of three things with increased eosinophils: allergy (especially asthma), a parasite, or a drug effect. Eosinophilia can rarely be neoplastic or autoimmune.
Marrow malignancy before anything else
Eosinophilia can be neoplastic, but only rarely; malignancy is a consideration if BASOPHILS are elevated. For eosinophils, think first of allergy, parasites and drug effects.
A.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slides 12, 13

A.io: Describe the process of bone marrow neoplasia
A.q: In leukemia, what can the peripheral white blood cell count be?
opts: High, because blasts spill into the blood
Some leukemias do show a high count, even hyperleukocytosis, but a high count is not required. Marrow involvement can suppress normal production, so the count may be low, normal or high.
Low, because blasts stay in the marrow
Marrow suppression can lower the count, but it is not the only pattern: the peripheral count in leukemia may be low, normal or high.
Normal until leukostasis develops
Leukostasis is impaired microcirculation with organ injury, and a high count alone does not establish it. The peripheral count in leukemia may be low, normal or high from the start.
Low, normal or high

Correct. The peripheral white blood cell count in leukemia may be low, normal or high, because marrow involvement can suppress normal blood-cell production while malignant cells may or may not spill into the blood.
A.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slides 21, 22

A.io: Compare and contrast acquired and innate immunity
A.q: Which defenses belong to innate immunity?
opts: Complement and interferons
Correct. Innate immunity acts without prior sensitization and includes skin and mucosal barriers, phagocytes, complement and interferons, with natural killer cells as its cytotoxic defense.
Memory B cells from a past exposure
Memory cells are adaptive: they exist only because of an earlier exposure, the opposite of innate defense.
Antibodies left by a past vaccine
Antibodies made after a vaccine are artificial active immunity, which is adaptive and needs sensitization.
Cytotoxic T cells with specific receptors
Antigen-specific T-cell receptors are adaptive. The innate cytotoxic defense is the natural killer cell.
A.cite: Immunity_Lecture_Recorded.pptx, Slide 13

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of acute coronary syndrome
A.q: What is the initiating feature of myocardial infarction?
opts: Gradual narrowing of the lumen over years
Gradual narrowing produces stable angina and allows collaterals to develop.
Vasospasm of an angiographically normal artery
Vasospasm is the mechanism of variant angina rather than the initiating feature of infarction.
Inflammation of the pericardium
Pericardial inflammation is a separate disease process. Infarction begins with thrombosis on a cracked plaque.
Thrombosis on an ulcerated or cracked atherosclerotic plaque
Correct. The plaque has to fail before the thrombus forms, which is why plaque stability matters more than plaque size.
A.cite: 6. Cardiac Pathophysiology for posting.pptx, Slide 38

A.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of vascular pathologies
A.q: What produces the color sequence in Raynaud phenomenon?
opts: Hemorrhage into the skin followed by resorption
The color change is due to changing perfusion and oxygenation rather than extravasated blood.
Deposition of immune complexes in dermal vessels
That would describe a vasculitic process rather than this vasospastic one.
Progressive thrombosis of digital arteries
The phenomenon is a reversible vasoconstrictive response rather than a thrombotic occlusion.
Vasoconstriction, anoxia, then reperfusion
Correct, and the sequence maps onto the colors in order: white to blue to red.
A.cite: SV Vascular Pathophys I Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 33

A.topic: Anemia by cell size and marrow response
A.io: Discuss the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of red blood cell disorders
A.q: Which deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia?
opts: Iron deficiency
Iron deficiency is a disorder of hemoglobin synthesis and sits in the MICROCYTIC group (early on, normocytic). The megaloblastic causes are vitamin B12 or folate deficiency.
Liver disease or alcohol
Liver disease and alcohol do cause macrocytosis, but they are listed as NONmegaloblastic causes. Megaloblastic anemia comes from vitamin B12 or folate deficiency.
Thalassemia
Thalassemia is a microcytic anemia, a disorder of hemoglobin synthesis. Megaloblastic (macrocytic) anemia comes from vitamin B12 or folate deficiency.
Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency

Correct. In the macrocytic group (mean cell volume above 100 fL, femtoliters), the megaloblastic causes are vitamin B12 or folate deficiency; liver disease, alcohol, drugs and reticulocytosis are the nonmegaloblastic causes.
A.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 33

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of different pulmonary diseases, including: Acute respiratory failure
A.q: How do fever, infection and burns contribute to hypercapnic ventilatory failure?
opts: They increase dead space
Increased dead space comes from hypovolemia, low cardiac output or pulmonary embolism.
They raise carbon dioxide production
Correct. Hypercapnic failure is alveolar ventilation inadequate for the carbon dioxide produced, and fever, infection and trauma or burns increase that production.
They block sensing of carbon dioxide
Blocked sensing of raised carbon dioxide is caused by drugs or alkalosis.
They cut the respiratory rate
A decreased respiratory rate reduces ventilation; fever, infection and burns act by raising carbon dioxide production.
A.cite: 9. Pulmonary Pathophysiology - Ward 2026 (rebuilt from recording).pptx, Slide 10

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of different pulmonary diseases, including: Restrictive pulmonary diseases
A.q: What is a pneumoconiosis?
opts: Lung disease from inhaled organic agents
Inhaled ORGANIC agents (wheat weevil, fungi, birds) cause hypersensitivity pneumonitis.
Granulomas from an unknown trigger
Granulomas to an unknown trigger describe sarcoidosis; pneumoconiosis is caused by inorganic dust.
Infection from aspirated flora
Aspirated oropharyngeal flora cause pneumonia and abscess; pneumoconiosis comes from inorganic dust.
Lung disease from inhaled inorganic dust
Correct. Pneumoconiosis is parenchymal lung disease caused by inhalation of inorganic dust particles such as coal, silica and asbestos.
A.cite: 9. Pulmonary Pathophysiology - Ward 2026 (rebuilt from recording).pptx, Slide 80

A.io: Compare and contrast the various subtypes and various functions of T lymphocytes
A.q: What is the main role of CD4 helper T cells?
opts: Killing infected cells with perforin
Perforin killing is the work of CD8 cytotoxic T cells; helpers coordinate rather than kill.
Coordinating humoral and cellular responses
Correct. CD4 helper T cells coordinate cell-mediated and humoral responses, using cytokines and cell contact to regulate other immune populations.
Secreting antibodies into plasma
Plasma cells secrete antibodies; helper signals support their differentiation.
Limiting activation to keep self-tolerance
Limiting immune activation and maintaining self-tolerance is the role of regulatory T cells.
A.cite: Immunity_Lecture_Recorded.pptx, Slides 24, 30

A.io: Describe the pathological processes and risk factors for the formation of coronary atherosclerosis and plaque
A.q: What do the macrophages within a plaque release?
opts: Collagen and fibrin, which stabilize the plaque
Collagen and fibrin form the stabilizing cap later, and are not what the macrophages release here.
Inflammatory mediators and growth factor

Correct. Both types of macrophage, including the lipid-filled foam cells, release inflammatory mediators and growth factor. These attract more leukocytes and stimulate smooth muscle proliferation, so the lesion keeps recruiting cells and wall growth.
Enzymes that clear the lipid core entirely
The lipid accumulates rather than being cleared; the macrophages release inflammatory mediators and growth factor instead.
Vasodilators that increase flow through the vessel
Vasodilation is not the described consequence. The mediators recruit more leukocytes and stimulate smooth muscle proliferation.
A.cite: 6. Cardiac Pathophysiology for posting.pptx, Slide 15

A.io: Describe the pathological processes and risk factors for the formation of coronary atherosclerosis and plaque
A.q: How do the capillaries within the atherosclerotic arterial wall contribute to disruption?
opts: They deliver macrophages that dissolve the fibrous cap
Bleeding and pressure build-up is the described mechanism rather than cap dissolution.
They drain lipid out of the core, collapsing the plaque
The described consequence is deposition and pressure rather than drainage.
Their thin walls bleed
Correct. The plaque can be disrupted from the inside as well as from the lumen, which is a route easy to overlook. Depositing blood products and raising pressure within the plaque.
They constrict, producing local ischemia within the wall
Constriction of these capillaries is not the described mechanism.
A.cite: 6. Cardiac Pathophysiology for posting.pptx, Slide 28

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of different pulmonary diseases, including: Restrictive pulmonary diseases
A.q: What characterizes the end-stage (destruction) pattern of diffuse interstitial lung disease?
opts: Lost alveolar walls and stiff, noncompliant lungs
Correct. The destruction stage is end-stage disease: alveolar walls are lost and the scarred lungs become stiff and noncompliant.
Hyperinflated lungs with air trapped in the sacs
Air trapped behind airways that lost their radial traction is emphysema, which hyperinflates the lungs rather than stiffening them.
Dilated bronchi that act as pockets of infection
Destroyed, dilated bronchi that hold infection are bronchiectasis, an airway disease rather than end-stage interstitial scarring.
Reversible inflammation filling the alveoli
Inflammation is the early, reversible pattern; the end stage is irreversible loss of alveolar walls.
A.cite: 9. Pulmonary Pathophysiology - Ward 2026 (rebuilt from recording).pptx, Slide 74

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of different pulmonary diseases, including: Obstructive pulmonary diseases
A.q: What feature defines the obstructive pulmonary diseases?
opts: Increased airflow resistance
Correct. Obstructive pulmonary diseases are manifested by increased airflow resistance, whether from the airway wall, loss of parenchyma or material in the lumen.
Decreased expansion of the lungs
Decreased expansion defines the RESTRICTIVE lung diseases; obstruction raises airflow resistance.
Thickening of the alveolar interstitium
Interstitial thickening is diffuse interstitial lung disease, a restrictive disorder.
Air in the pleural space
Air in the pleural space is pneumothorax, a pleural space disorder classed with the restrictive diseases.
A.cite: 9. Pulmonary Pathophysiology - Ward 2026 (rebuilt from recording).pptx, Slide 33

A.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of vascular pathologies
A.q: What is an aneurysm?
opts: Localized abnormal dilation of a blood vessel
Correct. It may be congenital or acquired, and it is classified by shape.
Blood tunneling through the medial planes of the wall
That is a dissection, where blood enters a defect in the arterial wall.
An intimal lesion projecting into the lumen
An intimal lesion projecting into the lumen is an atheroma, which narrows rather than dilating the vessel.
An irregular direct connection between artery and vein
That is an arteriovenous fistula, which bypasses the capillaries.
A.cite: SV Vascular Pathophys I Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 27

A.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of vascular pathologies
A.q: Which condition is linked to abnormal transforming growth factor signaling and defective collagen synthesis?
opts: Kawasaki disease
Kawasaki disease is a medium-vessel vasculitis rather than a connective tissue disorder.
Marfan syndrome
Correct, listed under poor connective tissue quality producing weak vessel walls — a genetic route to the same wall failure that hypertension reaches mechanically.
Systemic lupus erythematosus
Systemic lupus erythematosus appears under the immune complex small-vessel vasculitis subgroup instead.
Tertiary syphilis
Syphilis is listed under wall weakening through smooth muscle loss rather than under collagen synthesis defects.
A.cite: SV Vascular Pathophys I Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 28

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of coronary syndromes
A.q: Why is unstable angina included among the acute coronary syndromes?
opts: It always involves complete vessel occlusion
Complete occlusion is not what defines it. It is grouped with the acute syndromes because it may progress to acute ischemia.
It is caused by vasospasm rather than plaque
Vasospasm is the mechanism of Prinzmetal angina. Unstable angina is grouped as acute because it may progress.
It occurs only in patients with prior infarction
Prior infarction does not define it; it is included among the acute syndromes because it may progress to acute ischemia.
It may progress to acute ischemia
Correct. It is grouped by where it is heading rather than by where it currently is, which is the point of treating it as acute.
A.cite: 6. Cardiac Pathophysiology for posting.pptx, Slide 36

A.io: Compare and contrast the various types of blood cells and their roles in immunity
A.q: Which leukocyte is the most numerous first responder, acting by phagocytosis?
opts: Eosinophil
Eosinophils are linked with allergic reactions and parasitic invasion, not the first-responder role.
Basophil
Basophils are similar to tissue mast cells and much less numerous than neutrophils.
Neutrophil
Correct. Neutrophils, the “poly” or PMN (polymorphonuclear leukocyte), are the most numerous first responders and act by phagocytosis.
Monocyte
Monocytes are agranulocytes that enter tissue and become macrophages; the most numerous first responder is the neutrophil.
A.cite: Immunity_Lecture_Recorded.pptx, Slide 15

A.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of vascular pathologies
A.q: What follows injury to the vessel at the start of the atherosclerotic sequence?
opts: Accumulation of low-density lipoprotein in the vessel wall
Correct, and monocyte adhesion to the endothelium and platelet adhesion follow it before any smooth muscle is recruited.
Calcification of the extracellular matrix
Calcification comes at the END of the sequence, along with necrotic debris.
Smooth muscle proliferation with matrix production
That comes later, after smooth muscle has been recruited by factors from activated platelets and macrophages.
Formation of a fibrous cap over a lipid core
The mature plaque structure is the end product rather than the first step.
A.cite: SV Vascular Pathophys I Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 25

A.io: Review the anatomy of the vascular system
A.q: Which are named as superficial veins?
opts: The femoral and popliteal veins
Those are deep veins, where stasis in a dilated vein can produce thrombosis.
The portal and hepatic veins
Those are not among the superficial or deep veins named in this scheme.
The great and small saphenous veins
Correct, and the deep veins named are the femoral, popliteal and tibial. The anatomic location determines which pathology follows.
The jugular and subclavian veins
The jugular and subclavian veins are not the examples given for the superficial group in this scheme.
A.cite: SV Vascular Pathophys I Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 35

A.io: Discuss the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of red blood cell disorders
A.q: What does hypochromia of red cells reflect?
opts: Reduced hemoglobinization

Correct. The degree of hemoglobinization is reflected in the color of red cells: normochromic or hypochromic. Hypochromic cells carry less hemoglobin, as in the microcytic hypochromic anemias of impaired hemoglobin synthesis.
Reduced cell size
Reduced size is microcytosis, described by the size terms (normocytic, microcytic, macrocytic). Hypochromia is about color, the degree of hemoglobinization.
Abnormal cell shape
Shape is the third morphologic clue, separate from color. Hypochromia describes reduced hemoglobinization seen as paler red cells.
Increased cell volume
Increased volume is macrocytosis, a size term. Hypochromia is a color term: reduced hemoglobinization of the red cell.
A.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slides 31, 32

A.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of vascular pathologies
A.q: Raised blood pressure is a risk factor for which of these?
opts: Atherosclerosis, heart failure and renal failure
Correct. Raised blood pressure is a risk factor for atherosclerosis, congestive heart failure and renal failure, and also for cerebral hemorrhage and aortic dissection.
Varicose veins and hemorrhoids
Those follow chronic high INTRALUMINAL venous pressure with weakened wall support rather than systemic arterial hypertension.
Deep vein thrombosis
Deep vein thrombosis follows the Virchow triad rather than arterial hypertension.
Arteriovenous fistula
A fistula is a direct artery-to-vein connection arising from developmental defect, rupture, injury or inflammation.
A.cite: SV Vascular Pathophys I Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 20

A.io: Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivity reactions
A.q: The Arthus reaction and serum sickness are examples of which hypersensitivity type?
opts: Type I
Type I is IgE-mediated immediate hypersensitivity, as in anaphylaxis.
Type II
Type II is antibody bound to fixed cell or tissue antigens, as in ABO incompatibility.
Type III

Correct. Both are type III immune-complex reactions: the Arthus reaction is a local response in a previously sensitized person, and serum sickness is a systemic reaction to circulating immune complexes.
Type IV
Type IV is T-cell-mediated, as in contact dermatitis; the Arthus reaction and serum sickness are type III.
A.cite: Immunity_Lecture_Recorded.pptx, Slide 64

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of myopathies
A.q: What is restrictive cardiomyopathy most often related to?
opts: A specific clinical condition

Correct. Restrictive cardiomyopathy is most often related to a specific clinical condition such as amyloidosis. Whatever the cause, the myocardium becomes fibrotic, rigid and noncompliant, restricting diastolic filling.
Alcohol and pregnancy
These are factors in dilated cardiomyopathy. The restrictive form is usually related to a specific condition such as amyloidosis.
Coxsackievirus infection
Coxsackievirus relates to myocarditis. Restrictive cardiomyopathy is most often secondary to a condition such as amyloidosis.
Aging valvular calcification
Calcification produces valvular stenosis rather than restrictive cardiomyopathy.
A.cite: 6. Cardiac Pathophysiology for posting.pptx, Slide 65

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of different pulmonary diseases, including: Restrictive pulmonary diseases
A.q: Why does tension pneumothorax reduce cardiac output?
opts: Air enters the coronary arteries
The air stays in the pleural space; the problem is pressure pushing the mediastinum across.
The shifted mediastinum cuts venous return

Correct. Air enters but cannot escape on expiration and builds up under pressure; the ipsilateral lung collapses and the mediastinum is forced to the contralateral side, decreasing venous return and cardiac output.
The lung re-expands too quickly
The lung collapses, and air under pressure shifts the mediastinum.
Fluid tamponades the heart
Pleural air, not pericardial fluid, is the problem; mediastinal shift reduces venous return.
A.cite: 9. Pulmonary Pathophysiology - Ward 2026 (rebuilt from recording).pptx, Slides 90, 91

A.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of vascular pathologies
A.q: What do vascular smooth muscle cells synthesize?
opts: Immunoglobulins
Antibody production belongs to plasma cells rather than to vascular smooth muscle.
Clotting factors for the plasma
Most clotting factors are hepatic in origin rather than being synthesized by vascular smooth muscle.
Surfactant
Surfactant is produced by type II pneumocytes in the lung and has no vascular smooth muscle origin.
Collagen, elastin, proteoglycans and cytokines
Correct, which is why they are central to both repair and disease: the same synthetic capacity that rebuilds a wall also builds an atherosclerotic plaque. Growth factors too.
A.cite: SV Vascular Pathophys I Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 12

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of valvular stenosis, regurgitation, and prolapse
A.q: By what mechanism does rheumatic fever damage the heart?
opts: Direct invasion of the valve leaflets by the organism
Direct invasion describes infective endocarditis rather than rheumatic disease.
An immune attack arising from cross-reactivity after streptococcal infection
Correct. The organism is long gone; what damages the heart is the immune response aimed at something that resembles it.
Calcium deposition on the leaflets
Calcification is an age-related process rather than the rheumatic mechanism.
Ischemic necrosis of the papillary muscles
Papillary necrosis is a consequence of infarction rather than of rheumatic fever.
A.cite: 6. Cardiac Pathophysiology for posting.pptx, Slide 54

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of different pulmonary diseases, including: Cor pulmonale
A.q: Through which chain does chronic bronchitis lead to cor pulmonale?
opts: Left ventricular failure, pulmonary edema, right ventricular atrophy
Left ventricular failure raises left atrial pressure, but cor pulmonale is right ventricular DILATION driven by hypoxic pulmonary hypertension.
Embolism, dead space, hypercapnia, left atrial enlargement
Dead space and hypercapnia describe ventilatory failure; cor pulmonale is a right-heart consequence of pulmonary hypertension.
Hypoxic vasoconstriction, pulmonary hypertension, right ventricular dilation
Correct. Pulmonary artery vasoconstriction from hypoxia results in pulmonary hypertension, then right ventricular dilation (cor pulmonale) and right-sided heart failure.
Plaque rupture, coronary thrombosis, right ventricular infarction
That is a coronary story; cor pulmonale starts in the lung with hypoxic vasoconstriction.
A.cite: 9. Pulmonary Pathophysiology - Ward 2026 (rebuilt from recording).pptx, Slide 50

A.io: Compare and contrast primary and secondary immune response by the body
A.q: After a FIRST exposure to an antigen, which antibody class rises first?
opts: IgG
IgG starts rising later than IgM in the primary response; it dominates the secondary response.
IgM
Correct. On the primary response time course IgM rises and peaks first, and IgG starts later; on second exposure IgG dominates.
IgA
IgA is the mucosal class; the first class to rise after a first exposure is IgM.
IgE
IgE binds mast cells and basophils in allergy; it is not the early class of the primary response.
A.cite: Immunity_Lecture_Recorded.pptx, Slides 37, 46

A.io: Describe T-lymphocytes
A.q: Which surface marker is found on T cells as a group?
opts: CD3
Correct. T cells carry CD3, with CD4 or CD8 on the major subsets.
CD4
CD4 marks helper T cells and many regulatory T cells, not all T cells; CD3 is the marker across T cells.
CD8
CD8 marks only the cytotoxic subset; CD3 is the marker across T cells.
CD19
CD19 and CD20 are found on many B cells, so this marker points to a B lymphocyte rather than the cell asked about.
A.cite: Immunity_Lecture_Recorded.pptx, Slide 34

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of valvular stenosis, regurgitation, and prolapse
A.q: At what degree of closure does stenosis begin to affect hemodynamics?
opts: About ten percent
Hemodynamic effect is described from about fifty percent closure onwards.
About seventy-five percent

Seventy-five percent overshoots the threshold. Stenosis already affects hemodynamics at about fifty percent closure, where a pressure gradient across the valve begins to add pressure work for the heart.
About fifty percent

Correct. Hemodynamics are affected once the valve is about fifty percent closed. The narrowing creates a pressure gradient across the valve and extra pressure work, because blood must be forced through a smaller opening.
At complete closure
Effects appear well before complete closure, from about fifty percent.
A.cite: 6. Cardiac Pathophysiology for posting.pptx, Slide 43

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of pericarditidies
A.q: How does pericardial disease usually arise?
opts: As a primary condition in most cases
It is rarely primary; it is usually secondary to another cause, so the underlying condition drives the fluid in the sac and any inflammation of the pericardial structures.
Mainly as a consequence of myocardial infarction
Infarction is one possible primary cause among many rather than the main route; pericardial disease is usually secondary to any of various primary causes.
Secondary to another primary cause

Correct. Pericardial disease is rarely a primary condition and is usually secondary to another primary cause. Whatever the cause, fluid accumulates in the pericardial sac and painful inflammation of the pericardial structures occurs.
Mainly from direct infection of the pericardium
Causes are various rather than mainly infection, and pericardial disease is usually secondary to another primary cause, with fluid in the sac and painful inflammation whatever the cause.
A.cite: 6. Cardiac Pathophysiology for posting.pptx, Slide 67

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of white blood cell disorders
A.q: Why must both the relative and the absolute white cell counts be read?
opts: A fall in one type can falsely raise another's percentage

Correct. Percentages are shares of one total, so an absolute decrease in one cell type can show an artificially increased relative count in another. Reading the absolute count shows whether that cell really rose.
The relative count gives the number of cells per microliter
That describes the absolute count. The relative count is a percentage of the white cells; the absolute count, total white count times that fraction, is the number per microliter.
Each cell's percentage is measured apart from the others
The percentages are not independent: they are shares of one total, so when one cell type falls in absolute terms another's percentage can rise artificially. That is why both counts must be read.
The absolute count ignores the total white blood cell count
The absolute count is built from the total: white blood cell count times the cell's fraction. It is the relative percentage alone that can mislead when another cell type falls.
A.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 7

A.io: Compare and contrast the various etiologies and risk factors for coronary heart disease
A.q: What are the consequences of myocardial ischemia?
opts: Abnormal rhythm only, with function preserved throughout
Function is affected as well; the ischemic myocardium cannot contract normally.
Abnormal heart function and abnormal rhythm
Correct. Two immediate consequences and one that depends on duration, which is why time is the variable that decides how much muscle is lost. With irreversible damage if prolonged.
Immediate irreversible damage in every case
Damage becomes irreversible only if the ischemia is prolonged; brief ischemia does not kill the cell.
Valvular incompetence as the first consequence
Valve function is not the described consequence of myocardial ischemia.
A.cite: 6. Cardiac Pathophysiology for posting.pptx, Slide 4

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of valvular stenosis, regurgitation, and prolapse
A.q: What happens in mitral regurgitation?
opts: Blood flows from atrium to ventricle during systole
That is the normal direction of flow, and it occurs during diastole.
Blood leaks from the aorta into the ventricle during diastole
That describes aortic regurgitation. Mitral regurgitation sends blood back into the atrium during systole.
Flow across the valve is obstructed during diastole
Obstruction during diastole describes mitral stenosis. Regurgitation is backflow into the atrium during systole.
Blood flows back from ventricle to atrium during systole
Correct, and because the leak occurs during systole, part of every beat is wasted going the wrong way. Raising left atrial volume and pressure.
A.cite: 6. Cardiac Pathophysiology for posting.pptx, Slide 48

A.io: Review the anatomy of the vascular system
A.q: What does the adventitia contain?
opts: A single layer of endothelium on a basement membrane
A single endothelial layer on a basement membrane is the intima, the innermost of the three layers.
Lamellar units of elastin and smooth muscle
Lamellar units of elastin and smooth muscle describe the media of an elastic artery rather than the adventitia.
Nothing — it is a potential space
It is a real layer of loose connective tissue providing structural support.
Loose connective tissue, sometimes with nerve fibers
Correct, and in large vessels it carries its own small arterioles, which perfuse the adventitia and part of the media — the wall is too thick to be fed from the lumen alone.
A.cite: SV Vascular Pathophys I Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 10

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of different pulmonary diseases, including: Obstructive pulmonary diseases
A.q: Which cough pattern defines chronic bronchitis?
opts: Productive cough over 3 weeks after a viral illness
A cough outlasting a viral illness by weeks fits acute bronchitis, which can leave lasting hyperirritability.
Productive cough over 3 months a year for 2 years
Correct. Chronic bronchitis is hypersecretion of bronchial mucus with a chronic or recurrent productive cough of more than 3 months each year for 2 or more successive years.
Dry nighttime cough for 2 months
The defining cough is productive and recurs for more than 3 months a year over 2 or more years.
Purulent sputum from infected bronchial pockets
Purulent, foul-smelling sputum from dilated infected pockets is bronchiectasis.
A.cite: 9. Pulmonary Pathophysiology - Ward 2026 (rebuilt from recording).pptx, Slide 48

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of different pulmonary diseases, including: Pulmonary embolism
A.q: How does pulmonary embolism push toward hypercapnic ventilatory failure?
opts: It increases carbon dioxide production
Raised carbon dioxide production comes from fever, infection, trauma or burns, not from embolism.
It increases dead space
Correct. Increased dead space (wasted ventilation), from hypovolemia, low cardiac output or pulmonary embolism, leaves ventilation inadequate for the carbon dioxide produced.
It blunts sensing of carbon dioxide
Blunted sensing of raised carbon dioxide comes from drugs or alkalosis.
It blocks nerve signals to the muscles
Failure to signal the effectors is the Guillain-Barré syndrome and spinal cord injury route.
A.cite: 9. Pulmonary Pathophysiology - Ward 2026 (rebuilt from recording).pptx, Slides 10, 14

A.io: Define autoimmunity
A.q: Which T cells limit immune activation and maintain self-tolerance?
opts: Cytotoxic T cells
Cytotoxic T cells kill infected or malignant host cells; they do not restrain the response.
Helper T cells
Helper T cells coordinate and support responses; the restraining population is the regulatory T cell.
Regulatory T cells
Correct. Regulatory T cells limit immune activation and maintain self-tolerance; many are CD4 cells expressing FOXP3.
Memory T cells
Memory T cells carry forward a faster response on re-exposure; they do not maintain self-tolerance.
A.cite: Immunity_Lecture_Recorded.pptx, Slide 32

B.io: Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivity reactions
B.q: Which hypersensitivity type is mediated by IgE fixed on mast cells?
opts: Type I
Correct. Type I (anaphylactic, immediate) hypersensitivity: IgE made at a first exposure becomes fixed on mast cells and basophils, and re-exposure releases histamine and other substances.
Type II
Type II is antibody-mediated through IgG or IgM binding antigens on cells or within tissues.
Type III
Type III is immune-complex hypersensitivity: antigen–antibody complexes deposit in tissues or vessel walls.
Type IV
Type IV is mediated by sensitized CD4 or CD8 T cells, not by antibody.
B.cite: Immunity_Lecture_Recorded.pptx, Slides 60, 61

B.io: Describe the antigens’ ability to promote an immune response
B.q: What starts the antigen-dependent phase of B-cell maturation?
opts: Expression of surface IgM
Surface IgM is expressed in the earlier, antigen-INDEPENDENT phase of maturation.
Release of perforin
Perforin release belongs to cytotoxic T cells killing their targets, not to B-cell maturation.
Exposure to the antigen
Correct. The antigen-dependent phase, in which the B cell differentiates into a plasma cell making specific antibody, is initiated by exposure to the antigen.
Processing in the thymus
Thymic processing is how T lymphocytes mature; B cells mature in the bone marrow.
B.cite: Immunity_Lecture_Recorded.pptx, Slide 22

B.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of vascular pathologies
B.q: Which layer are smooth muscle cells the predominant element of?
opts: The intima
The healthy intima is an endothelial monolayer; smooth muscle appears there only as pathology, in intimal thickening.
The media
Correct, and their dual role is the point: they are important in normal vascular repair AND play a large part in the development of atherosclerosis.
The adventitia
The adventitia is loose connective tissue providing support.
The basement membrane
The basement membrane supports the endothelium rather than being a cellular layer.
B.cite: SV Vascular Pathophys I Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 12

B.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of vascular pathologies
B.q: Which conditions raise the risk of coagulation in deep vein thrombosis?
opts: Cancer, sepsis, lupus and oral estrogen
Correct, and the increased coagulability may be genetic or acquired — these four are the acquired examples given.
Immobility and mechanical compression
Those act through reduced flow and increased venous pressure respectively.
Dehydration and thrombocytosis
Dehydration and thrombocytosis are grouped under increased blood viscosity, a risk factor separate from the increased coagulation group of cancer, sepsis, lupus and oral estrogen.
Trauma and intravenous drug use
Trauma and intravenous drug use fall under mechanical injury rather than increased coagulability.
B.cite: SV Vascular Pathophys I Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 37

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of pericarditidies
B.q: What causes most acute pericarditis?
opts: Most follow myocardial infarction
Infarction is one cause rather than the commonest. Most acute pericarditis is idiopathic, and most of that is viral.
Most are idiopathic
Correct. The two statements sit together: unexplained in the sense that nothing is identified, but viral in most of those cases. Most of those are viral.
Most follow cardiac surgery
Surgery is one cause rather than the commonest. Most acute pericarditis is idiopathic, and most of those cases are viral.
Most are bacterial
Viral causes predominate among the idiopathic majority, which is itself most of acute pericarditis.
B.cite: 6. Cardiac Pathophysiology for posting.pptx, Slide 70

B.io: Describe the pathological processes and risk factors for the formation of coronary atherosclerosis and plaque
B.q: What is the significance of a large lipid core within a plaque?
opts: A large core makes the plaque more stable
The opposite is described: a large lipid core makes the plaque fragile and liable to rupture.
Plaques with large lipid cores are fragile and rupture
Correct. Size and stability run in opposite directions, which is why the dangerous plaque is not necessarily the one narrowing the lumen most.
A large core prevents platelet aggregation
Rupture of such a plaque exposes subendothelial proteins and initiates platelet aggregation.
A large core indicates the plaque has been cleared
The core is accumulated lipid and debris rather than evidence of clearance.
B.cite: 6. Cardiac Pathophysiology for posting.pptx, Slide 15

B.io: Describe the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of coagulation disorders
B.q: What initiates physiologic coagulation?
opts: Factor XII on contact
Factor XII belongs to the intrinsic factors the aPTT (activated partial thromboplastin time) assesses in the laboratory. Physiologic initiation is tissue factor-VIIa activating IX and X.
External bleeding
External bleeding is not required. Physiologic coagulation is initiated when tissue factor-VIIa activates factors IX and X.
Thrombin on fibrinogen
Thrombin acting on fibrinogen is the fibrin-formation step at the END of the reactions. Initiation is tissue factor-VIIa activating IX and X.
Tissue factor with factor VIIa
Correct. Physiologic initiation is tissue factor-VIIa activating factors IX and X; external bleeding is not required.
B.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slides 43, 44

B.io: Describe the function of the complement system
B.q: Which three main functions does complement serve?
opts: Antibody secretion, memory, opsonization
Antibody secretion is the plasma cell's work and memory belongs to lymphocytes; only opsonization is a complement function.
Antigen presentation, lysis, memory
Antigen presentation and memory are lymphocyte and antigen-presenting cell functions.
Opsonization, inflammation, membrane attack

Correct. Complement opsonizes targets for phagocytes, generates inflammatory mediators that recruit and activate immune cells, and forms the membrane attack complex that damages susceptible membranes.
Neutralization, agglutination, precipitation
These are antibody functions; complement adds opsonization, inflammation and membrane attack.
B.cite: Immunity_Lecture_Recorded.pptx, Slides 67, 75

B.io: Review the anatomy of the blood cells
B.q: Which appearance identifies a band neutrophil on a smear?
opts: Kidney-bean nucleus indented over half its width
Correct. A band neutrophil has a kidney-bean nucleus with mature chromatin and no nucleoli, an indentation greater than half the diameter, and secondary granules only.
Two-lobed nucleus with large red secondary granules
A nucleus with two lobes and red secondary granules is the eosinophil. The band neutrophil has a single kidney-bean nucleus indented more than half its width.
Round nucleus with scant pale cytoplasm, no granules
A round mature nucleus with clumped chromatin and scant light blue cytoplasm without granules is the lymphocyte. The band has a kidney-bean nucleus indented more than half its width.
Two to three lobes hidden by dark granules
A mature nucleus of two to three lobes obscured by numerous basophilic granules is the basophil. The band neutrophil has one kidney-bean nucleus indented more than half its width.
B.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slides 10, 12, 13, 14

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of valvular stenosis, regurgitation, and prolapse
B.q: What is a primary cause of valvular stenosis?
opts: Infective endocarditis and papillary muscle rupture
These cause regurgitation rather than stenosis. Stenosis follows rheumatic scarring or valvular calcification with aging.
Post-inflammatory scarring from rheumatic fever

Correct. Post-inflammatory scarring from rheumatic fever is one of the two primary causes of stenosis; the other is valvular calcification with aging. The narrowed opening forces the heart to do extra pressure work.
Homocysteine-induced vascular injury
That mechanism relates to atherosclerosis rather than to valves.
Coxsackievirus infection of the valve leaflets
Coxsackievirus relates to myocarditis. Stenosis follows rheumatic scarring or age-related calcification.
B.cite: 6. Cardiac Pathophysiology for posting.pptx, Slide 43

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of different pulmonary diseases, including: Restrictive pulmonary diseases
B.q: What is the characteristic lesion of sarcoidosis?
opts: Caseating granulomas with necrosis
The granulomas of sarcoidosis are NONcaseating: uniform, epithelioid and surrounded by large histiocytes.
Hyaline membranes in the alveoli
Hyaline membranes are protein deposits of acute respiratory distress syndrome, not granulomas.
Subpleural apical blebs
Small subpleural blebs at the apices are the source of primary spontaneous pneumothorax, not the lesion of sarcoidosis.
Noncaseating epithelioid granulomas
Correct. Sarcoidosis develops multiple, uniform, noncaseating epithelioid granulomas, most commonly in the lymph nodes and lung, surrounded by large histiocytes.
B.cite: 9. Pulmonary Pathophysiology - Ward 2026 (rebuilt from recording).pptx, Slide 76

B.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of vascular pathologies
B.q: What triggers renin secretion?
opts: A rise in pressure in the afferent arterioles
Renin is secreted in response to a DECREASE in blood pressure rather than an increase.
A rise in plasma sodium concentration
The described trigger is the pressure change at the afferent arteriole.
A fall in pressure in the afferent arterioles
Correct. The kidney senses the pressure drop at the afferent arteriole and responds, which is the first step of the sequence that restores it.
Direct sympathetic stimulation of the adrenal medulla
Renin comes from the kidney, and the named trigger is the afferent arteriolar pressure.
B.cite: SV Vascular Pathophys I Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 19

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of different pulmonary diseases, including: Obstructive pulmonary diseases
B.q: What does a low FEV1/FVC (forced expiratory volume in 1 second to forced vital capacity) ratio identify?
opts: A restrictive pattern
Restriction is confirmed by a low total lung capacity, not by a low ratio.
Incomplete emptying
Incomplete emptying is shown by a high residual volume, a separate finding.
A gas-transfer problem
A reduced DLCO (diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide) raises the gas-transfer question.
Expiratory airflow limitation
Correct. A low FEV1/FVC (forced expiratory volume in 1 second to forced vital capacity) ratio identifies expiratory airflow limitation, the obstructive pattern.
B.cite: 9. Pulmonary Pathophysiology - Ward 2026 (rebuilt from recording).pptx, Slide 59

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of white blood cell disorders
B.q: How is a relative white cell count converted to an absolute count?
opts: Divide the cell's percentage by the total white count
Dividing gives a meaningless small number. The conversion multiplies: total white blood cell count times the relative count as a fraction gives cells per microliter.
Subtract the lymphocyte count from the total white count
Subtraction would lump every non-lymphocyte together. Each cell's absolute count is found by multiplying the total white blood cell count by that cell's relative fraction.
Multiply the total white count by the cell's fraction
Correct. The absolute count is the white blood cell count times the relative count expressed as a fraction: a total of 8,000 cells/µL with 25 percent neutrophils gives 2,000 neutrophils/µL.
Read the cell's percentage straight off the differential
The percentage is the relative count itself, not the absolute one. To get cells per microliter, multiply the total white blood cell count by that percentage as a fraction.
B.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 7

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of valvular stenosis, regurgitation, and prolapse
B.q: What happens to left ventricular stroke volume in mitral stenosis?
opts: It increases to compensate
Reduced filling means the ventricle cannot raise its stroke volume.
It is unchanged until the valve closes completely
Stroke volume falls as the gradient worsens, because the ventricle is not being filled.
It becomes dependent on atrial contraction alone
The described consequence is a decreased left ventricular stroke volume, from inadequate filling.
It decreases
Correct. The ventricle is not diseased; it is simply not being filled, which is why the problem is upstream of it.
B.cite: 6. Cardiac Pathophysiology for posting.pptx, Slide 46

B.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of vascular pathologies
B.q: What is the consequence of endothelial repair for nitric oxide?
opts: Its production increases sharply
The change described runs the other way, toward decreased production.
It is unchanged by injury
Decreased nitric oxide production is specifically named as a consequence.
It is replaced by carbon monoxide signaling
No such substitution is described; the named consequence is simply decreased nitric oxide production.
Its production decreases
Correct, and because nitric oxide is a vasodilator and an inhibitor of platelet adhesion, losing it shifts the vessel toward constriction and thrombosis.
B.cite: SV Vascular Pathophys I Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 13

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of white blood cell disorders
B.q: What is bandemia?
opts: More immature neutrophils in the blood
Correct. Bandemia is an increase in immature (band) neutrophils, a left shift, which may accompany infection or other inflammatory stress.
More mature neutrophils in the blood
A rise in mature neutrophils is neutrophilia. Bandemia specifically means more IMMATURE neutrophils, the band forms, in the circulation: a left shift.
Fewer than 200 neutrophils/µL
That is agranulocytosis, profound neutropenia. Bandemia is an increase, not a loss: more immature band neutrophils in the blood.
More eosinophils from a drug effect
A drug effect is one of the three things to think of with eosinophilia. Bandemia concerns neutrophils: an increase in their immature band forms.
B.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 10

B.io: Compare and contrast the functions of the various types of antibodies and the various mechanisms by which antibodies destroy antigens
B.q: Which antibodies are usually present in the plasma of a group O person?
opts: Anti-A without anti-B
Anti-A without anti-B is the usual plasma pattern of group B, whose red cells carry B.
Anti-A and anti-B
Correct. Group O red cells carry neither A nor B antigen, and group O plasma usually carries both anti-A and anti-B.
Anti-B without anti-A
Anti-B without anti-A is the usual plasma pattern of group A, whose red cells carry A.
Neither anti-A nor anti-B
Lacking both antibodies is group AB, whose red cells carry both A and B.
B.cite: Immunity_Lecture_Recorded.pptx, Slide 49

B.io: Compare and contrast the functions of the various types of antibodies and the various mechanisms by which antibodies destroy antigens
B.q: How does neutralization protect without destroying the target?
opts: It clumps the targets into lattices
Clumping antigen-bearing particles is agglutination; neutralization blocks an interaction and leaves the target intact.
It blocks an essential host interaction
Correct. Antibody binding blocks an essential interaction with a host cell, preventing viral attachment or entry or a toxin reaching its target, and limits activity without physical destruction.
It coats the targets for phagocytes
Coating to ease ingestion is opsonization, which leads to the target being engulfed.
It assembles pores in their membranes
Pore assembly is the complement membrane attack complex, which does destroy the target by lysis.
B.cite: Immunity_Lecture_Recorded.pptx, Slide 50

B.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of vascular pathologies
B.q: Which sex and age groups are listed as at risk?
opts: Premenopausal women specifically
The listed group is POSTmenopausal women, which suggests the opposite.
Children and adolescents
Risk rises with increasing age rather than falling on the young.
Men only, at any age
Postmenopausal women are named alongside men, so the risk is not confined to one sex.
Men and postmenopausal women
Correct, together with increasing age — the pairing implies that the premenopausal state is relatively protective.
B.cite: SV Vascular Pathophys I Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 24

B.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms involved in immune processes
B.q: What keeps lymph moving along the larger lymphatic vessels?
opts: Muscle movement, breathing and arterial pulsation
Correct. Skeletal muscle movement, pressure changes in the thorax during breathing and the pulsations of adjacent arteries help propel lymph, while the vessel's valves keep it moving forward.
Contraction of the heart alone
Lymph has no central pump. It is propelled by skeletal muscle movement, breathing-related pressure changes and the pulsation of nearby arteries.
Gravity draining it down toward the feet
That reverses the direction: lymph returns toward the circulation, and physical activity or passive movement keeps it flowing at a decent pace.
Cilia beating along the lymphatic lumen
No cilia line the lymphatic vessel. Its internal valves keep lymph moving forward, and outside forces such as muscle movement push it along.
B.cite: Immunity_Lecture_Recorded.pptx, Slide 8

B.io: Compare and contrast primary and secondary immunodeficiency including the genetic basis
B.q: Which defect underlies X-linked agammaglobulinemia?
opts: Abnormal thymic development
Variable impairment of thymic and T-cell development is DiGeorge syndrome.
Impaired B-cell maturation
Correct. X-linked agammaglobulinemia is impaired B-cell maturation with very low antibodies, and is associated with recurrent pyogenic bacterial infections.
Profound T-cell dysfunction
Profound T-cell dysfunction with impaired B-cell immunity is severe combined immunodeficiency.
Medication-induced loss of function
Reduced function from medications is secondary immunodeficiency; X-linked agammaglobulinemia is primary, with a genetic basis.
B.cite: Immunity_Lecture_Recorded.pptx, Slide 76

B.io: Discuss the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of red blood cell disorders
B.q: Which anemia results from diminished erythropoiesis?
opts: Hereditary spherocytosis
Hereditary spherocytosis is a hemolytic anemia: rigid spherocytes are destroyed in the spleen. Aplastic anemia is the anemia of diminished erythropoiesis here.
Anemia of acute blood loss
Blood-loss anemia is loss of formed cells, and the marrow answers with an increased reticulocyte response. Aplastic anemia is a failure of production.
Extravascular hemolytic anemia
Extravascular hemolysis is premature destruction within phagocytes. Aplastic anemia is the anemia of diminished erythropoiesis.
Aplastic anemia

Correct. The anemias of diminished erythropoiesis are megaloblastic anemia, vitamin B12 deficiency anemia, iron deficiency anemia and aplastic anemia: too little production rather than loss or destruction.
B.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 40

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of different pulmonary diseases, including: Obstructive pulmonary diseases
B.q: Why do the lungs in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease fail to deflate normally?
opts: Air is trapped in damaged air sacs
Correct. The lungs do not deflate like normal lungs because air is trapped in damaged air sacs, while bronchioles narrow and block with mucus.
The pleural space fills with air
Air in the pleural space is a pneumothorax, a separate disorder that collapses the lung.
Surfactant production rises
Surfactant comes from type II pneumocytes; its LOSS causes collapse in acute respiratory distress syndrome.
The alveolar walls stiffen with fibrosis
Fibrotic stiff alveoli belong to restrictive interstitial disease, not to air trapping.
B.cite: 9. Pulmonary Pathophysiology - Ward 2026 (rebuilt from recording).pptx, Slides 30, 32, 55

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of myopathies
B.q: What defines dilated cardiomyopathy?
opts: Cardiac failure with dilation of one or both ventricular chambers
Correct. It is named for the chamber change, and the causes listed for it are otherwise unrelated to one another.
A thickened, hyperkinetic ventricular muscle mass
That describes hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. The dilated form is cardiac failure with dilation of one or both ventricles.
A stiff, fibrotic ventricle with impaired filling
That describes restrictive cardiomyopathy. The dilated form is failure with dilation of one or both ventricles.
Inflammation with leukocyte infiltration and necrosis
That describes myocarditis. Dilated cardiomyopathy is cardiac failure with chamber dilation.
B.cite: 6. Cardiac Pathophysiology for posting.pptx, Slide 63

B.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of vascular pathologies
B.q: How is atherosclerosis characterized as a process?
opts: A purely degenerative process of aging
It is described as an active inflammatory and healing response rather than passive degeneration.
A chronic inflammatory and healing response

Correct. Atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory and healing response of the arterial wall to endothelial injury, which then progresses through lipoprotein accumulation, cell recruitment, lipid accumulation and calcification.
An infectious process of the arterial wall
Direct pathogen invasion of vessel walls is a vasculitis mechanism rather than the atherosclerotic one.
A congenital malformation of the intima
The process is acquired, beginning with injury to a previously healthy vessel.
B.cite: SV Vascular Pathophys I Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 25

B.io: Describe the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of myeloproliferative syndromes
B.q: What kind of disorder is polycythemia vera?
opts: An erythropoietic response to hypoxia
A marrow response to hypoxia or raised erythropoietin is SECONDARY erythrocytosis, a reaction to a stimulus. Polycythemia vera is a clonal myeloproliferative neoplasm.
A fall in plasma from dehydration
Reduced plasma volume with normal red-cell mass is relative erythrocytosis. Polycythemia vera is an absolute increase from a clonal myeloproliferative neoplasm.
A clonal myeloproliferative neoplasm

Correct. Polycythemia vera is a clonal myeloproliferative neoplasm: an absolute erythrocytosis from clonal proliferation of myeloid cells, listed with chronic myeloid leukemia, essential thrombocythemia and primary myelofibrosis.
A myelodysplastic marrow neoplasm
Myelodysplastic neoplasms show ineffective hematopoiesis with cytopenias, the opposite of an excess. Polycythemia vera is a clonal myeloproliferative neoplasm.
B.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slides 41, 18

B.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of vascular pathologies
B.q: What happens to the aortic wall in dissection?
opts: The intima thickens progressively, narrowing the lumen
Intimal thickening that narrows the lumen happens in the inner layer; a dissection instead splits the laminar planes of the media to form a blood-filled channel in the wall.
The media calcifies without affecting the lumen
Medial calcification leaves the lumen unchanged and the layers together; a dissection instead splits the laminar planes of the media into a blood-filled channel within the aortic wall.
The whole circumference dilates uniformly
That describes a fusiform aneurysm rather than a dissection.
The laminar planes of the media split apart
Correct, and hypertension is the major risk factor, though Marfan syndrome and inflammation can also produce it. A blood-filled channel forms within the wall.
B.cite: SV Vascular Pathophys I Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 29

B.io: Compare and contrast the various types of blood cells and their roles in immunity
B.q: Besides circulating monocytes, what is another origin of resident tissue macrophages?
opts: Development before birth, then local renewal
Correct. Monocytes enter tissue during inflammation and become macrophages, but some resident macrophages develop before birth and renew locally.
Neutrophils settling in inflamed tissue
Neutrophils are the first-responder granulocytes that act by phagocytosis; they never become macrophages, which come from monocytes or develop before birth.
Lymphoblasts maturing in the thymus
The thymus processes T lymphocytes; macrophages come from monocytes, or develop before birth and renew locally.
B cells changing after antigen exposure
B cells become plasma cells and memory cells after antigen exposure, never macrophages.
B.cite: Immunity_Lecture_Recorded.pptx, Slide 18

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of valvular stenosis, regurgitation, and prolapse
B.q: What is a prerequisite for infective endocarditis?
opts: Pre-existing calcification of the valve
Pre-existing valve pathology matters for the subacute form, but bloodstream invasion is the prerequisite.
A recent myocardial infarction
Infarction is not a prerequisite. Invasion of the bloodstream is, since the valve is reached through the blood.
Invasion of the bloodstream by the organism
Correct. The valve is reached through the blood, so bacteremia has to come first.
Immune cross-reactivity with streptococcal antigens
That mechanism belongs to rheumatic heart disease. Infective endocarditis requires bloodstream invasion by the organism.
B.cite: 6. Cardiac Pathophysiology for posting.pptx, Slide 56

B.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of blood disorders
B.q: In acute leukemia, acquired mutations in which genes block the differentiation of immature cells?
opts: Immunoglobulin genes
Rearranging immunoglobulin genes is NORMAL B-cell development (V(D)J recombination in the marrow). Maturation arrest comes from acquired mutations in transcription factors.
Coagulation factor genes
Coagulation-factor genes are not tied to leukemic maturation arrest. In acute leukemia, the block in differentiation comes from acquired mutations in transcription factors.
Red-cell membrane genes
Red-cell membrane genes are not tied to leukemic maturation arrest. The block in differentiation of immature lymphoid or myeloid cells comes from acquired mutations in transcription factors.
Transcription factor genes
Correct. Acquired mutations in transcription factors, which regulate the differentiation of immature lymphoid or myeloid cells, produce the maturation arrest of acute leukemia.
B.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 20

B.topic: Anemia by cell size and marrow response
B.io: Discuss the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of red blood cell disorders
B.q: Early iron deficiency usually falls in which mean cell volume group?
opts: Microcytic
Iron deficiency becomes microcytic once established, but the early stage is listed in the normocytic group (80 to 100 fL, femtoliters).
Normocytic
Correct. Established iron deficiency is microcytic, but EARLY iron deficiency is listed with the normocytic anemias (mean cell volume 80 to 100 fL, femtoliters), before the cells have shrunk.
Macrocytic
Macrocytic anemias come from vitamin B12 or folate deficiency or from liver disease, alcohol, drugs or reticulocytosis. Early iron deficiency is normocytic.
Megaloblastic
Megaloblastic anemia is the vitamin B12 or folate subset of the macrocytic group. Early iron deficiency is normocytic, later microcytic.
B.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 33

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of different pulmonary diseases, including: Restrictive pulmonary diseases
B.q: Which of the three alveolar patterns of diffuse interstitial lung disease is reversible?
opts: Inflammation
Correct. The immune response shows three patterns: inflammation (early and reversible), fibrosis, and destruction (end stage).
Fibrosis
Fibrosis, with fibroblast proliferation and heavy collagen deposition, follows the reversible inflammatory stage.
Destruction
Destruction is the end-stage pattern, with loss of alveolar walls and stiff lungs.
Bullae formation
Bullae form from trapped air in emphysema, not as an interstitial pattern.
B.cite: 9. Pulmonary Pathophysiology - Ward 2026 (rebuilt from recording).pptx, Slides 72, 73, 74
