B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of different pulmonary diseases, including: Acute respiratory failure
B.q: On room air, which arterial oxygen tension (PaO2) defines the hypoxemia of acute respiratory failure?
opts: Below 40 mmHg
Lower than the defining value; acute respiratory failure is set at an arterial oxygen below 60 mmHg on room air.
Below 50 mmHg
Fifty mmHg is the carbon dioxide threshold (above 50); the oxygen threshold is below 60 mmHg.
Below 60 mmHg
Correct. Acute respiratory failure is disturbed gas exchange with arterial oxygen below 60 mmHg, carbon dioxide above 50 mmHg or pH below 7.30, breathing room air (21% oxygen).
Below 70 mmHg
Higher than the defining value; the threshold is an arterial oxygen below 60 mmHg.
B.cite: 9. Pulmonary Pathophysiology - Ward 2026 (rebuilt from recording).pptx, Slide 7

B.io: Compare and contrast examples of autoimmune diseases
B.q: Lupus is an example of which hypersensitivity type?
opts: Type I
Type I is IgE- and mast cell-mediated allergy and anaphylaxis.
Type II
Type II examples are ABO incompatibility and anti-glomerular basement membrane disease.
Type III
Correct. Lupus is a type III immune-complex example, alongside immune-complex glomerulonephritis or arthritis.
Type IV
Type IV examples are contact dermatitis, tuberculosis-related reactions and transplant rejection.
B.cite: Immunity_Lecture_Recorded.pptx, Slide 64

B.io: Compare and contrast the various etiologies and risk factors for coronary heart disease
B.q: Which are given as uncommon causes of coronary heart disease?
opts: Coronary vasospasm and thrombosis
These are common mechanisms acting on a narrowed vessel rather than the uncommon causes.
Reduced oxygen content of the blood, and poor perfusion
Correct. Both reach the same endpoint from outside the coronary artery: the vessel may be open, but what flows through it either carries too little oxygen or arrives at too low a pressure.
Familial hypercholesterolemia and high fat diet
These are mechanisms of abnormal lipid metabolism contributing to atherosclerosis, not the uncommon causes listed.
Rheumatic fever and infective endocarditis
These damage valves rather than causing coronary heart disease.
B.cite: 6. Cardiac Pathophysiology for posting.pptx, Slide 8

B.io: Describe the pathological processes and risk factors for the formation of coronary atherosclerosis and plaque
B.q: What determines the risk that a plaque will rupture?
opts: Its age alone
Age is not given as the determinant; composition and mechanical stress are.
Its composition and mechanical stress
Correct. Rupture risk depends on the composition of the plaque and on the mechanical stresses that act on it. A vulnerable plaque has a large necrotic core covered by a thin fibrous cap.
The degree of luminal narrowing alone
Severe stenosis is one of the vulnerability features, but composition and stress are what determine rupture risk.
The lipoprotein that delivered the lipid
Which lipoprotein delivered the lipid is not described as determining rupture.
B.cite: 6. Cardiac Pathophysiology for posting.pptx, Slide 26

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of different pulmonary diseases, including: Restrictive pulmonary diseases
B.q: When does community-acquired pneumonia develop?
opts: After 4 days in hospital
Pneumonia starting after 4 hospital days is late-onset hospital-acquired pneumonia; community-acquired covers symptoms that begin within 48 hours of admission.
When normal defenses are compromised
Correct. Normal defenses (immune responses, cough reflex, sneezing, mucociliary clearance) protect the lung; community-acquired pneumonia occurs when they are compromised.
When surfactant is overproduced
Surfactant excess is not a cause; compromised defenses let microorganisms multiply.
When the pleural space fills with air
Air in the pleural space is pneumothorax, a restrictive pleural space disorder, not this mechanism.
B.cite: 9. Pulmonary Pathophysiology - Ward 2026 (rebuilt from recording).pptx, Slides 106, 108, 109

B.io: Review the anatomy of the blood cells
B.q: Approximately what share of whole blood is plasma?
opts: 35 percent
Too low. Whole blood is about 55 percent plasma and 45 percent formed elements, so 35 percent understates the fluid fraction by roughly 20 points.
45 percent

This is the share of the formed elements (red cells, white cells and platelets), not of plasma. Whole blood is about 55 percent plasma and 45 percent formed elements; the two figures are easy to swap.
55 percent
Correct. Whole blood is approximately 55 percent plasma and 45 percent formed elements, and plasma itself is about 90 to 92 percent water carrying electrolytes, nutrients, wastes and proteins.
65 percent
Too high. Plasma is about 55 percent of whole blood, with the formed elements making up the remaining 45 percent. A 65 percent plasma share would leave the cells at only about a third.
B.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 3

B.io: Describe the process of bone marrow neoplasia
B.q: How does multiple myeloma produce hypercalcemia?
opts: Renal injury from monoclonal proteins
Monoclonal proteins injure the kidneys, but that is the renal consequence. Hypercalcemia comes from altered bone remodeling, the same process that makes osteolytic lesions.
Marrow infiltration crowding red cells
Marrow infiltration explains the anemia of myeloma. Hypercalcemia comes from altered bone remodeling with osteolytic lesions.
Altered bone remodeling

Correct. In myeloma, altered bone remodeling can produce osteolytic lesions and hypercalcemia; the monoclonal proteins and marrow infiltration separately cause renal injury, anemia and impaired immunity.
Impaired immunity from abnormal antibodies
Impaired immunity is another consequence of the monoclonal proteins and marrow infiltration. Hypercalcemia arises from altered bone remodeling.
B.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 27

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of different pulmonary diseases, including: Pulmonary malignancies
B.q: Which lung carcinoma grows fastest, doubling in about 33 days?
opts: Adenocarcinoma
Adenocarcinoma is slower, doubling its size in about 180 days.
Small cell carcinoma
Correct. Small cell (oat cell) carcinoma grows rapidly, doubling in about 33 days, with common widespread metastasis and paraneoplastic syndrome.
Squamous cell carcinoma
Squamous cell carcinoma doubles its volume in about 100 days.
Large cell carcinoma
Large cell carcinoma doubles in size about every 100 days, three times slower than small cell.
B.cite: 9. Pulmonary Pathophysiology - Ward 2026 (rebuilt from recording).pptx, Slides 25, 26, 27

B.io: Compare and contrast the morphology of the various types of antibodies
B.q: What determines an immunoglobulin's class?
opts: The heavy-chain constant region
Correct. The heavy-chain constant region determines immunoglobulin class (heavy chain mu, delta, gamma, epsilon or alpha).
Whether the light chain is kappa or lambda
Every class can carry kappa or lambda light chains; class is set by the heavy chain.
The variable-region sequence
Variable regions decide WHAT the antibody binds, not its class.
The number of disulfide bonds
Disulfide bonds connect chains and support structure; they do not define class.
B.cite: Immunity_Lecture_Recorded.pptx, Slide 41

B.io: Discuss the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of red blood cell disorders
B.q: What is relative erythrocytosis?
opts: An increase in red-cell mass
An increased red-cell mass is ABSOLUTE erythrocytosis. Relative erythrocytosis has no extra red cells: the plasma volume is reduced.
A clonal myeloproliferative neoplasm
A clonal myeloproliferative neoplasm raising red-cell mass is polycythemia vera, an absolute erythrocytosis. Relative erythrocytosis is reduced plasma volume.
A marrow response to hypoxia
An erythropoietic response to hypoxia or increased erythropoietin is secondary erythrocytosis, which raises red-cell mass. Relative erythrocytosis is reduced plasma volume.
Less plasma without more red-cell mass
Correct. Relative erythrocytosis is reduced plasma volume without increased red-cell mass, such as dehydration; hemoglobin and hematocrit rise only because the plasma has shrunk.
B.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 41

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of different pulmonary diseases, including: Obstructive pulmonary diseases
B.q: What happens to the airways in acute bronchitis?
opts: Destruction of alveolar walls without fibrosis
Alveolar wall destruction without fibrosis is emphysema; acute bronchitis inflames the trachea and bronchi.
Permanent dilation of the bronchi
Persistent bronchial dilation from destroyed walls is bronchiectasis.
Inflammation, more mucus, lost ciliary function
Correct. In acute bronchitis the airways are inflamed, narrow and swollen, with increased mucus, loss of ciliary function and loss of portions of the ciliated epithelium.
Gland hypertrophy over successive years
Bronchial gland hypertrophy over years of productive cough is chronic bronchitis.
B.cite: 9. Pulmonary Pathophysiology - Ward 2026 (rebuilt from recording).pptx, Slides 45, 47

B.io: Review the functions of the components of the vascular system
B.q: Which four functions does the vascular system serve?
opts: Gas exchange and the production of blood cells
Gas exchange happens at the capillary interface, but cell production is a marrow function rather than one of the four named vascular roles.
Immune surveillance and antibody synthesis
Antibody synthesis belongs to lymphoid tissue. The vascular system transports rather than manufactures.
Transport of nutrients, wastes, hormones; homeostasis
Correct. Nutrients go to tissues, wastes come away from them, hormones travel from one part of the body to another, and fluid balance is maintained across all tissues so cells can function.
Thermoregulation and acid production
Neither is among the four functions named for the vascular system.
B.cite: SV Vascular Pathophys I Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 5

B.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of vascular pathologies
B.q: What does a nonthrombogenic endothelial surface achieve?
opts: It accelerates clot formation at rest
The healthy surface does the opposite, resisting thrombosis until it is injured.
It prevents leukocytes from entering tissues anywhere
The endothelium regulates inflammation rather than blocking it outright.
It stops all molecules crossing the vessel wall
Exchange across the wall is a central vascular function rather than something the endothelium prevents.
It keeps blood in a fluid state
Correct, and it is an active property rather than a passive one, which is why endothelial injury is the event that lets platelets adhere and a thrombus begin.
B.cite: SV Vascular Pathophys I Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 12

B.io: Explain the pathophysiology of cardiac ischemia
B.q: What is the immediate metabolic consequence of reduced oxygen supply to cardiac cells?
opts: The formation of adenosine triphosphate falls
Correct. The cell loses its energy currency first, and everything that follows -- failure to contract, then death -- is downstream of that.
Lactate is converted back into glucose within the cell
The described consequence is a fall in energy production rather than gluconeogenesis.
Calcium is actively pumped out of the cell more rapidly
Active transport requires the energy that is now in short supply.
Oxygen extraction from the blood falls
Extraction is not the described first consequence; the shortfall is in supply relative to demand.
B.cite: 6. Cardiac Pathophysiology for posting.pptx, Slide 30

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of different pulmonary diseases, including: Pulmonary embolism
B.q: Which condition is associated with an EXUDATIVE pleural effusion?
opts: Severe heart failure
Severe heart failure produces a transudate through raised hydrostatic pressure.
Nephrotic syndrome
Nephrotic syndrome produces a transudate through lowered oncotic pressure.
Pulmonary embolism
Correct. Exudates are associated with malignancies, infections, pulmonary embolism, sarcoidosis, post-myocardial infarction syndrome and pancreatic disease.
Cirrhosis with ascites
Cirrhosis with ascites produces a transudate; exudates come with embolism, malignancy and infection.
B.cite: 9. Pulmonary Pathophysiology - Ward 2026 (rebuilt from recording).pptx, Slides 94, 95

B.io: Define the concept of hypersensitivity
B.q: What defines hypersensitivity?
opts: Immune reactions that injure the body
Correct. Hypersensitivity is when immune reactions, either humoral or cellular, result in injury to the body; four types are seen.
Any immune response to a foreign antigen
Most immune responses protect without injury; hypersensitivity is the subset that harms the body.
Failure to produce enough antibody
Too little immune function is immunodeficiency, such as X-linked agammaglobulinemia.
Infection with a pyogenic organism
Infection is the threat itself; hypersensitivity is injury caused by the immune reaction.
B.cite: Immunity_Lecture_Recorded.pptx, Slide 60

B.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of vascular pathologies
B.q: What is vasculitis?
opts: Vessel wall thickening with loss of elasticity
Wall thickening with loss of elasticity is arteriosclerosis, not the vessel wall inflammation that defines vasculitis.
Dilation of a vessel from wall weakening
Dilation of a vessel from wall weakening is an aneurysm rather than inflammation of the wall.
Thrombus formation within a deep vein
That is deep vein thrombosis, which arises from the Virchow triad rather than from inflammation of the wall as a primary event.
Wall inflammation, mostly small vessels
Correct — arterioles, capillaries and venules, although any organ and any vessel can be affected. Manifestations follow from the location of the vessel involved.
B.cite: SV Vascular Pathophys I Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 32

B.io: Review the anatomy of the vascular system
B.q: How does capillary diameter compare with a red blood cell?
opts: About ten times larger
A capillary is at most the width of a single red cell rather than many times it.
About a hundred times larger
A hundredfold difference is far off: a capillary is equal to or even slightly smaller than the diameter of a red blood cell, with an endothelial lining and no media.
Too variable to compare
The comparison is specific: equal to or slightly smaller than a red blood cell.
Equal to or even slightly smaller
Correct. A capillary is equal to or even slightly smaller than a red blood cell, and it has no media: just an endothelial lining for exchange.
B.cite: SV Vascular Pathophys I Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 11

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of different pulmonary diseases, including: Restrictive pulmonary diseases
B.q: What ruptures in a primary spontaneous pneumothorax?
opts: A bronchus from penetrating trauma
Chest injury is a typical setting for tension pneumothorax; a primary pneumothorax comes from ruptured apical blebs.
A cyst from preexisting lung disease
Rupture of a cyst or bleb in preexisting lung disease is SECONDARY pneumothorax.
The thoracic duct
Thoracic duct leakage of chyle causes chylothorax, a pleural effusion.
Small subpleural blebs at the apices
Correct. Primary pneumothorax results from rupture of small subpleural blebs in the apices: air enters the pleural space, the lung collapses and the rib cage springs out.
B.cite: 9. Pulmonary Pathophysiology - Ward 2026 (rebuilt from recording).pptx, Slides 88, 89

B.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of pulmonary pathologies
B.q: What thickens the walls of small pulmonary vessels in pulmonary hypertension?
opts: Lipid plaques in the intima
Lipid-rich plaque is atherosclerosis; here the intima becomes fibrotic and the media gains muscle.
Thinning of the media
The media thickens rather than thins, from increased muscle mass.
More muscle mass in the media
Correct. Chronic exposure thickens the small pulmonary vessel walls through increased muscle mass of the media, driven by local tissue hypoxia and acidosis, and the intima becomes fibrotic.
Calcium in the adventitia
No calcification is described; the change is medial muscle mass with intimal fibrosis.
B.cite: 9. Pulmonary Pathophysiology - Ward 2026 (rebuilt from recording).pptx, Slide 23

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of pericarditidies
B.q: Which effusion type follows heart failure or hypoproteinemia?
opts: A chylous collection
Chylous fluid follows obstruction to lymphatic drainage. Heart failure and hypoproteinemia produce a serous transudate.
A serous transudate
Correct. Both causes act by altering the forces governing fluid movement rather than by injuring anything.
A hemopericardium
Frank blood follows penetrating cardiac trauma. Heart failure and hypoproteinemia produce a serous transudate.
A serosanguinous effusion
That follows blunt trauma, surgery or resuscitation. Heart failure and hypoproteinemia produce a serous transudate.
B.cite: 6. Cardiac Pathophysiology for posting.pptx, Slide 68

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of acute coronary syndrome
B.q: On what does the result of vessel occlusion depend?
opts: Collateral circulation
Correct. The same occlusion in two hearts produces different damage, which is why the vessel alone does not predict the outcome. Workload and the length of time.
The lipoprotein pattern of the patient
Lipoproteins relate to plaque formation rather than to the consequence of an occlusion.
Which valve is nearest the occluded segment
Valve proximity is not a determinant. The result depends on collateral circulation, workload and how long the occlusion lasts.
The presence of pericardial fluid
Pericardial fluid is not a determinant here. Collateral circulation, workload and duration are what decide the result.
B.cite: 6. Cardiac Pathophysiology for posting.pptx, Slide 39

B.io: Compare and contrast the various types of blood cells and their roles in immunity
B.q: Which form immediately precedes the segmented neutrophil?
opts: Band form
Correct. The neutrophil line runs promyelocyte, myelocyte, metamyelocyte, then the band form, then the segmented neutrophil.
Metamyelocyte
The metamyelocyte comes one step earlier; it matures into the band form, which then becomes the segmented neutrophil.
Myelocyte
The myelocyte is two steps earlier: myelocyte, metamyelocyte, band, then segmented neutrophil.
Monoblast
The monoblast belongs to a different line, ending in the monocyte rather than the neutrophil.
B.cite: Immunity_Lecture_Recorded.pptx, Slide 14

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of different pulmonary diseases, including: Asthma
B.q: Which finding fits non-allergic (intrinsic) asthma?
opts: An IgE-mediated immediate phase
An IgE-mediated immediate phase defines allergic (extrinsic) asthma.
A more favorable prognosis
Intrinsic asthma has the LESS favorable prognosis and frequently develops in middle age.
A specific allergen identified
No specific allergen can be identified in intrinsic asthma; it is precipitated by exercise, stress and irritants.
Negative skin tests, normal serum IgE
Correct. Intrinsic asthma has no identifiable specific allergen, negative skin tests to common inhalant allergens and normal serum IgE; it often develops in middle age.
B.cite: 9. Pulmonary Pathophysiology - Ward 2026 (rebuilt from recording).pptx, Slide 37

B.io: Describe the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of coagulation disorders
B.q: Hemophilia A is a deficiency of which factor?
opts: Factor IX
Factor IX deficiency is hemophilia B. Hemophilia A is factor VIII deficiency.
Factor V
Factor V is the factor altered in factor V Leiden, a genetic thrombophilia, not a bleeding deficiency. Hemophilia A is factor VIII deficiency.
Factor VIII
Correct. Hemophilia A is factor VIII deficiency; hemophilia B is factor IX deficiency. Both factors work together, IXa with its cofactor VIIIa activating factor X.
Factor VII
Factor VII is the extrinsic factor the PT (prothrombin time) assesses. Hemophilia A is factor VIII deficiency.
B.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 46

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of valvular stenosis, regurgitation, and prolapse
B.q: What are the early valve changes of rheumatic endocardial inflammation?
opts: Immediate calcification of the leaflets
Calcification is an age-related process rather than the rheumatic sequence.
Valvular swelling and erosions

Correct. Endocardial inflammation causes valvular swelling and erosions, with platelet aggregation and fibrin on the leaflets. Scarring and shortening of the valvular structures appear only with progression, which is why rheumatic fever is a cause of stenosis.
Ballooning of the leaflets into the atrium
That describes prolapse. Rheumatic inflammation produces swelling and erosion, then scarring and shortening.
Rupture of the papillary muscles
Papillary rupture is a cause of acute regurgitation rather than the rheumatic sequence.
B.cite: 6. Cardiac Pathophysiology for posting.pptx, Slide 55

B.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of vascular pathologies
B.q: Which three are named as weakening the wall through smooth muscle loss or inappropriate matrix synthesis?
opts: Ischemia, hypertension and tertiary syphilis
Correct, and they form one of three routes to wall failure, alongside poor connective tissue quality and an imbalance of collagen degradation against synthesis.
Marfan syndrome, lupus and rheumatoid arthritis
Marfan belongs to the connective tissue quality group, and the other two are immune complex vasculitides.
Smoking, diabetes and hyperlipidemia
Those are atherosclerosis risk factors; smoking is separately listed as predisposing to aortic aneurysm.
Giant cell arteritis, polyarteritis nodosa and Kawasaki disease
Giant cell arteritis, polyarteritis nodosa and Kawasaki disease are vasculitides classified by vessel size.
B.cite: SV Vascular Pathophys I Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 28

C.io: Define the function and specific types of antigens
C.q: What does an adaptive B-cell or T-cell receptor recognize?
opts: Patterns shared by groups of organisms
That describes innate receptors, which recognize patterns shared by groups of organisms rather than one epitope.
Any foreign protein, whatever its shape
Adaptive receptors are specific: each recognizes a particular epitope, not any foreign protein.
A particular epitope
Correct. Adaptive specificity means B-cell and T-cell receptors recognize particular epitopes, the specific regions of an antigen.
Antigens met in a previous exposure
Recognition does not require prior exposure; memory only makes the response faster and stronger on re-exposure.
C.cite: Immunity_Lecture_Recorded.pptx, Slide 10

C.io: Review the anatomy of the blood cells
C.q: Which progenitor gives rise to megakaryocytes?
opts: Lymphoid progenitor
The lymphoid progenitor gives B cells, T cells and natural killer cells, none of which make platelets. Megakaryocytes sit on the myeloid branch with erythroid precursors, granulocytes and monocytes.
Myeloid progenitor

Correct. In the simplified lineage model the multipotent stem cell gives myeloid and lymphoid progenitors, and the myeloid progenitor gives erythroid precursors, megakaryocytes (which make platelets), granulocytes and monocytes.
Erythroid precursor
The erythroid precursor is a sister product of the myeloid progenitor, and it matures into erythrocytes. Megakaryocytes come from the myeloid progenitor directly and make platelets.
Granulocyte precursor
The granulocyte line gives neutrophils, eosinophils and basophils. Megakaryocytes are a separate product of the myeloid progenitor, and they make platelets rather than granulocytes.
C.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 5

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of myopathies
C.q: Which factors are associated with dilated cardiomyopathy?
opts: Amyloidosis
Amyloidosis is given in relation to restrictive cardiomyopathy.
Aortic valve calcification
Valve calcification produces stenosis rather than dilated cardiomyopathy.
Streptococcal cross-reactivity
That mechanism belongs to rheumatic heart disease. Dilated cardiomyopathy is associated with alcohol, genetics, pregnancy and a post-viral state.
Alcohol, genetics, pregnancy and a post-viral state
Correct. Four causes with nothing obvious in common, which is why the condition is grouped by what the ventricle does rather than by what caused it.
C.cite: 6. Cardiac Pathophysiology for posting.pptx, Slide 63

C.io: Compare and contrast natural and artificial immunity
C.q: What makes vaccination a form of ARTIFICIAL active immunity?
opts: Antibodies come from another source
Receiving preformed antibodies from another source is passive immunity, such as tetanus or rabies immune globulin.
The antigen is met through ordinary contact
Contact with the antigen in the ordinary course of life makes active immunity natural rather than artificial.
It acts with no prior sensitization
Defenses that act without prior sensitization are innate. Vaccination works by sensitizing the body to the antigen.
Antigen exposure is done on purpose
Correct. Active immunity is acquired by the body's own processes after exposure to the antigen; it is artificial when the exposure is deliberate, as with vaccination.
C.cite: Immunity_Lecture_Recorded.pptx, Slide 11

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of white blood cell disorders
C.q: How is an absolute neutrophil count of 750 cells/µL graded?
opts: Agranulocytosis
Agranulocytosis needs a count below 200 cells/µL. At 750 the count sits in the moderate band, 500 to 1,000 cells/µL.
Severe neutropenia
Severe neutropenia is below 500 cells/µL. A count of 750 is above that line, in the moderate band of 500 to 1,000.
Moderate neutropenia
Correct. An absolute neutrophil count of 750 cells/µL falls in the moderate band, 500 to 1,000 cells/µL; severe is below 500 and mild is 1,000 to 1,500.
Mild neutropenia
Mild neutropenia is 1,000 to 1,500 cells/µL. A count of 750 is below that band, in moderate neutropenia (500 to 1,000).
C.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 9

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of white blood cell disorders
C.q: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is a neoplasm of which cells?
opts: Precursor B cells
Precursor B cells (lymphoblasts) give B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is a neoplasm of MATURE B cells.
Mature B cells
Correct. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is a mature B-cell neoplasm, related to small lymphocytic lymphoma (CLL/SLL).
Mature T cells
Mature T and natural killer cells give their own distinct neoplasms. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is a neoplasm of mature B cells.
Plasma cells
A malignancy of differentiated plasma cells is myeloma. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia arises from mature B cells and is related to small lymphocytic lymphoma.
C.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slides 23, 28

C.io: Review the anatomy of the blood cells
C.q: What does the mean cell volume measure?
opts: The average hemoglobin mass per red cell
Average hemoglobin content (mass) per red cell is the mean cell hemoglobin. Mean cell volume measures the cell's size: the average volume of a red cell.
The hemoglobin concentration in packed cells
The average concentration of hemoglobin in a given volume of packed red cells is the mean cell hemoglobin concentration. Mean cell volume is the average volume of one red cell.
The share of blood volume that is red cells
The proportion of blood volume occupied by red cells is the hematocrit, a whole-blood measure. Mean cell volume is the average volume of a single red cell.
The average volume of a red cell
Correct. Mean cell volume is the average volume of a red cell; it sorts anemias into microcytic (below 80 fL, femtoliters), normocytic (80 to 100 fL) and macrocytic (above 100 fL).
C.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slides 30, 33

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of valvular stenosis, regurgitation, and prolapse
C.q: What is the difference between valvular stenosis and regurgitation?
opts: Stenosis is failure to close, regurgitation is failure to open
The definitions are the other way round: stenosis is failure to open completely, regurgitation failure to close completely.
Both describe failure of the valve to open
They describe opposite failures: stenosis is failure to open, regurgitation failure to close.
Stenosis affects only the mitral valve and regurgitation only the aortic
Both can affect either valve. The distinction is between failing to open and failing to close.
Stenosis is failure to open completely, regurgitation is failure to close completely
Correct, and the consequence follows directly: one makes the heart push harder, the other makes it push more.
C.cite: 6. Cardiac Pathophysiology for posting.pptx, Slide 42

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of different pulmonary diseases, including: Pulmonary hypertension
C.q: How does mitral stenosis lead to pulmonary hypertension?
opts: It increases pulmonary blood flow
Increased pulmonary blood flow comes from left-to-right shunts such as atrial septal defect and patent ductus arteriosus.
It causes hypoxic vasoconstriction
Hypoxic vasoconstriction is the route in chronic bronchitis and advanced emphysema.
It raises left atrial pressure
Correct. Mitral stenosis, mitral regurgitation and left ventricular failure cause pulmonary hypertension by increasing left atrial pressure.
It raises blood viscosity
Raised viscosity is the polycythemia route; mitral stenosis raises left atrial pressure.
C.cite: 9. Pulmonary Pathophysiology - Ward 2026 (rebuilt from recording).pptx, Slide 22

C.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of vascular pathologies
C.q: What is Monckeberg medial sclerosis?
opts: Lipid plaque formation with a necrotic core
Lipid plaque with a necrotic core is atherosclerosis, the most clinically relevant form of arteriosclerosis.
Calcification of the media of muscular arteries
Correct. It is calcification of the medial walls of muscular arteries, one of the four patterns of arteriosclerosis, and it is usually not clinically significant.
Hyaline thickening of arterioles from hypertension
That is one of the small-vessel subtypes rather than medial calcification.
Inflammatory destruction of the vessel wall
Inflammatory destruction of the wall is vasculitis, an entirely different category from medial calcification.
C.cite: SV Vascular Pathophys I Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 22

C.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of vascular pathologies
C.q: What defines a dissection?
opts: Localized abnormal dilation of the vessel
Localized abnormal dilation is an aneurysm, in which the wall bulges rather than splitting into layers.
Inflammation of the vessel wall with leukocyte infiltration
Inflammation of the wall with leukocyte infiltration is vasculitis rather than a blood-filled wall channel.
Blood enters a wall defect and tunnels through medial planes
Correct — through medial or medial-adventitial planes. The vessel is not merely dilated; its wall has been split into layers by blood under pressure.
Calcification of the media without luminal change
Calcification of the media without luminal change does not define a dissection, in which blood enters a wall defect and tunnels through medial or medial-adventitial planes.
C.cite: SV Vascular Pathophys I Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 27

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of valvular stenosis, regurgitation, and prolapse
C.q: Which organisms most commonly cause infective endocarditis?
opts: Coxsackievirus and adenovirus
Coxsackievirus relates to myocarditis. Endocarditis is most often streptococcal strains or Staphylococcus aureus.
Candida alone
Candida appears among the less virulent causes of the subacute form rather than as the commonest cause.
Group A streptococcus through immune cross-reactivity
Cross-reactivity is the rheumatic mechanism rather than direct infection.
Streptococcal strains and Staphylococcus aureus
Correct. The same two names recur, with the less virulent organisms reserved for the subacute form on an already damaged valve.
C.cite: 6. Cardiac Pathophysiology for posting.pptx, Slide 56

C.io: Describe the etiologies and pathophysiological processes for angina pectoris
C.q: What distinguishes angina pectoris from infarction at the cellular level?
opts: The ischemia is intermittent and insufficient to kill cardiac cells
Correct. Same mechanism, different endpoint: the supply falls short but recovers before the cells are lost.
The ischemia affects only the right ventricle
Location is not what separates them. Angina is ischemia intermittent and insufficient to kill cardiac cells.
There is no ischemia, only abnormal conduction
Angina is defined by ischemia; what distinguishes it is that the ischemia stops short of killing cells.
Cell death occurs but is confined to the endocardium
Cell death is precisely what angina does not produce; that is what separates it from infarction.
C.cite: 6. Cardiac Pathophysiology for posting.pptx, Slide 34

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of different pulmonary diseases, including: Obstructive pulmonary diseases
C.q: What defines emphysema?
opts: Alveolar wall destruction without fibrosis
Correct. Emphysema (type A chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, the “pink puffer”) is destruction of alveolar walls without fibrosis and abnormal enlargement of distal air sacs.
Alveolar wall thickening with fibrosis
Thickened, fibrotic alveolar walls describe interstitial lung disease, a restrictive disorder.
Reversible airway inflammation
Reversible obstruction with airway inflammation is asthma; emphysema is irreversible alveolar destruction.
Permanent dilation of the bronchi
Permanent bronchial dilation is bronchiectasis; emphysema enlarges the distal air sacs instead.
C.cite: 9. Pulmonary Pathophysiology - Ward 2026 (rebuilt from recording).pptx, Slide 53

C.io: Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivity reactions
C.q: Which of these is a T-cell-mediated hypersensitivity reaction?
opts: Anaphylaxis to insect venom
Anaphylaxis is type I, mediated by IgE on mast cells; insect venoms are one trigger.
Contact dermatitis
Correct. Contact dermatitis is type IV, mediated by sensitized CD4 or CD8 T cells, along with tuberculosis-related reactions and T-cell-mediated transplant rejection.
ABO transfusion incompatibility
ABO incompatibility is type II, antibody against red-cell antigens.
Serum sickness
Serum sickness is type III, a systemic reaction to circulating immune complexes.
C.cite: Immunity_Lecture_Recorded.pptx, Slide 65

C.io: Describe the process of bone marrow neoplasia
C.q: Which consequences do monoclonal proteins and marrow infiltration cause in myeloma?
opts: Renal injury, anemia and impaired immunity
Correct. In multiple myeloma, monoclonal proteins and marrow infiltration can cause renal injury, anemia and impaired immunity; altered bone remodeling adds osteolytic lesions and hypercalcemia.
Leukostasis in the lungs and brain

Leukostasis is impaired microcirculation from a high white-cell burden, often in the lungs or brain. Myeloma's monoclonal proteins and marrow infiltration cause renal injury, anemia and impaired immunity.
Thrombosis with a falling platelet count
Thrombosis despite a falling platelet count is immune heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. Myeloma's proteins and marrow infiltration cause renal injury, anemia and impaired immunity.
Raised hematocrit from plasma loss
A hematocrit raised by reduced plasma volume is relative erythrocytosis. Myeloma's marrow infiltration causes anemia, along with renal injury and impaired immunity.
C.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 27

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of different pulmonary diseases, including: Restrictive pulmonary diseases
C.q: What injury starts acute respiratory distress syndrome?
opts: Rupture of subpleural blebs
Ruptured subpleural blebs cause primary spontaneous pneumothorax.
Damage to the alveolar-capillary membrane
Correct. Acute respiratory distress syndrome begins with damage to the alveolar-capillary membrane, giving widespread alveolar infiltrates and severe dyspnea.
Loss of radial traction on airways
Lost radial traction is emphysema; acute respiratory distress syndrome starts at the alveolar-capillary membrane.
Closure of the collapsible pharynx
Pharyngeal closure during sleep is obstructive sleep apnea, not alveolar-capillary membrane damage.
C.cite: 9. Pulmonary Pathophysiology - Ward 2026 (rebuilt from recording).pptx, Slide 84

C.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of vascular pathologies
C.q: What combination is essential hypertension suspected to arise from?
opts: Small changes in renal sodium handling and vessel tone

Correct. Essential hypertension is suspected to arise from a combination of small changes in renal sodium homeostasis and in vessel wall tone or structure, so the abnormality is suspected to be distributed across two systems rather than located in one.
A single inherited defect in the renin gene
No single genetic lesion is proposed; the mechanism is a combination of small changes.
Autoimmune destruction of the vascular endothelium
No autoimmune mechanism is described for essential hypertension.
Chronic infection of the arterial wall
Direct invasion of vessel walls by pathogens is a mechanism of vasculitis rather than of essential hypertension.
C.cite: SV Vascular Pathophys I Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 20

C.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of vascular pathologies
C.q: Which two blood-borne events accompany the neointimal response?
opts: Red cell aggregation and hemolysis
Red cell aggregation and hemolysis are not among the named components of the neointimal response.
Eosinophil degranulation and mast cell activation
The cells named are platelets and leukocytes generally rather than these allergic effectors.
Plasma cell infiltration with antibody deposition
Immune complex deposition characterizes certain vasculitides rather than the general neointimal response.
Platelet activation and leukocyte recruitment
Correct: a thrombus forms and the inflammatory cascade begins at the injury site, so the response is simultaneously thrombotic and inflammatory.
C.cite: SV Vascular Pathophys I Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 13

C.io: Compare and contrast the functions of the various types of antibodies and the various mechanisms by which antibodies destroy antigens
C.q: What is precipitation, as an antibody function?
opts: Clumping antigen-bearing cells
Clumping cells or particles that carry surface antigen is agglutination.
Cross-linking soluble antigens
Correct. Antibodies cross-link soluble antigens into larger complexes that can become insoluble and precipitate, which may help phagocytes clear them.
Coating a cell for ingestion
A coating that eases ingestion by phagocytes is opsonization, not precipitation of soluble antigen.
Blocking a virus's attachment
Blocking viral attachment or entry is neutralization; precipitation cross-links soluble antigen.
C.cite: Immunity_Lecture_Recorded.pptx, Slide 54

C.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of vascular pathologies
C.q: By what two routes does angiotensin II raise blood pressure?
opts: Raising heart rate and respiratory rate
Respiratory rate plays no part, and the described routes are vascular tone and aldosterone.
Increasing red cell mass and blood viscosity
Increasing red cell mass and blood viscosity are not among the described actions of angiotensin II.
Dilating the efferent arteriole to raise filtration
Angiotensin II is a vasoconstrictor, and the routes named are smooth muscle tone and aldosterone.
Raising smooth muscle tone, and driving aldosterone
Correct — one route acts on resistance immediately, the other on volume through increased renal sodium resorption, so both determinants of pressure are addressed.
C.cite: SV Vascular Pathophys I Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 19

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of different pulmonary diseases, including: Restrictive pulmonary diseases
C.q: Under which group of restrictive disorders is acute respiratory distress syndrome classified?
opts: Fibrotic interstitial diseases
The fibrotic interstitial diseases are diffuse interstitial lung disease, sarcoidosis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis and occupational disease.
Pleural space disorders
Pleural space disorders are pneumothorax and pleural effusion.
Neuromuscular and chest wall disorders
These are Guillain-Barré syndrome, myasthenia gravis, kyphoscoliosis, flail chest and obstructive sleep apnea.
Atelectatic parenchymal disorders
Correct. Acute (adult) and infant respiratory distress syndromes are the atelectatic disorders of the lung parenchyma.
C.cite: 9. Pulmonary Pathophysiology - Ward 2026 (rebuilt from recording).pptx, Slides 67, 68

C.io: Compare and contrast the various types of blood cells and their roles in immunity
C.q: What does a monocyte become once it enters tissue during inflammation?
opts: A plasma cell
Plasma cells come from B lymphocytes and produce antibodies; monocytes become macrophages.
A mast cell
Mast cells are the tissue cells basophils resemble; a monocyte entering tissue becomes a macrophage.
A neutrophil
Neutrophils are granulocytes that mature through the band form; a monocyte that enters tissue becomes a macrophage.
A macrophage
Correct. Monocytes circulate in blood and enter tissues during inflammation, where tissue signals promote differentiation into macrophages.
C.cite: Immunity_Lecture_Recorded.pptx, Slide 18

C.io: Compare and contrast the various etiologies and risk factors for coronary heart disease
C.q: Atherosclerosis narrows the coronary lumen. Which processes does that narrowing predispose to?
opts: Valvular calcification and regurgitation
Valve disease is a separate process and is not a consequence of coronary narrowing.
Pericardial effusion and tamponade
Pericardial disease is not precipitated by coronary narrowing.
Thrombosis, coronary vasospasm and endothelial cell dysfunction
Correct. The narrowing is the setting rather than the whole disease: what precipitates an event is one of these three acting on an already narrowed vessel.
Myocardial leukocyte infiltration and necrosis without vessel involvement
That describes myocarditis, which is not a consequence of coronary atherosclerosis.
C.cite: 6. Cardiac Pathophysiology for posting.pptx, Slide 8

C.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of vascular pathologies
C.q: Which risk factor for deep vein thrombosis reflects reduced blood flow?
opts: Dehydration
Dehydration acts by increasing blood VISCOSITY rather than by reducing flow.
Immobility
Correct, and it sits alongside increased venous pressure, mechanical injury, increased blood viscosity, anatomic variations and increased coagulability.
Oral estrogen
Estrogen acts through increased risk of coagulation, alongside cancer, sepsis and lupus.
Surgery
Surgery is listed under mechanical injury, with trauma and intravenous drug use.
C.cite: SV Vascular Pathophys I Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 37

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of different pulmonary diseases, including: Restrictive pulmonary diseases
C.q: For a patient already hospitalized for another reason, within what time of admission must respiratory symptoms begin for the pneumonia to count as community-acquired?
opts: Under 12 hours
Too short: patients hospitalized for under 48 hours before respiratory symptoms are still called community-acquired.
Under 24 hours
Too short: patients hospitalized under 48 hours before symptoms are still community-acquired.
Under 48 hours
Correct. Patients hospitalized for other reasons for under 48 hours before respiratory symptoms develop are also called community-acquired.
Under 96 hours
Too long: 4 hospital days defines EARLY hospital-acquired pneumonia; community-acquired is under 48 hours.
C.cite: 9. Pulmonary Pathophysiology - Ward 2026 (rebuilt from recording).pptx, Slides 108, 109

C.io: Compare and contrast the various types of blood cells and their roles in immunity
C.q: From which precursor do lymphocytes arise?
opts: Myeloblast
The myeloblast is a granulocyte precursor, giving the eosinophil and the basophil; lymphocytes come from the lymphoblast.
Monoblast
The monoblast gives rise to the monocyte, the other agranulocyte, not the lymphocyte.
Lymphoblast
Correct. In blood cell formation the hematopoietic stem cell gives rise to the lymphoblast, which becomes the lymphocyte.
Megakaryocyte
The megakaryocyte, from the promegakaryocyte, sheds platelets; it plays no part in making lymphocytes.
C.cite: Immunity_Lecture_Recorded.pptx, Slide 14

C.io: Describe the function of the complement system
C.q: How does the membrane attack complex kill a target cell?
opts: It triggers apoptosis with granzymes
Granzyme-triggered apoptosis is the cytotoxic T cell's mechanism.
It disrupts ionic and osmotic balance
Correct. The pores damage the membrane and disrupt ionic and osmotic balance; ions and water move abnormally, and severe disruption leads to cell lysis.
It coats the cell for phagocytes
Coating for phagocytes is opsonization, done by C3b rather than the terminal complex.
It blocks the cell's receptor binding
Blocking an essential interaction is antibody neutralization.
C.cite: Immunity_Lecture_Recorded.pptx, Slides 68, 74

C.io: Explain the pathophysiology of cardiac ischemia
C.q: Which factors are described as impairing coronary perfusion?
opts: Plaques, thrombosis, vasospasm, microcirculation, pressure
Correct. Five different ways to arrive at the same shortfall, only one of which is the fixed narrowing people picture first.
Increased heart rate and contractility, acting alone
These raise demand rather than impairing supply; they are on the workload side.
Valvular stenosis and regurgitation, acting alone
Valve disease increases cardiac workload rather than impairing coronary perfusion directly.
Pericardial inflammation
Pericardial disease is not among the described causes of impaired coronary perfusion.
C.cite: 6. Cardiac Pathophysiology for posting.pptx, Slide 30

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of valvular stenosis, regurgitation, and prolapse
C.q: What is the central hemodynamic abnormality in mitral stenosis?
opts: An abnormal gradient during systole
The mitral valve is open during diastole, so the gradient appears then.
An abnormal left atrial to left ventricular pressure gradient during diastole
Correct. The atrium stays at higher pressure than the ventricle through diastole, and the gradient widens as the stenosis worsens.
Backflow from the ventricle into the atrium during systole
That describes mitral regurgitation. Mitral stenosis produces an atrial to ventricular gradient during diastole.
Obstruction to outflow from the left ventricle
That describes aortic stenosis. Mitral stenosis obstructs filling and produces a diastolic gradient.
C.cite: 6. Cardiac Pathophysiology for posting.pptx, Slide 45

C.io: Compare and contrast the functions of the various types of antibodies and the various mechanisms by which antibodies destroy antigens
C.q: Which pair of antibody effects acts on a soluble toxin?
opts: Opsonization and lysis
Opsonization and lysis act on cells such as bacteria, whose surfaces carry antigenic determinants.
Agglutination and opsonization
Agglutination needs antigen on particles or cells; a soluble toxin has no surface to clump.
Agglutination and lysis
Both need a cell or particle surface; a soluble toxin is neutralized and precipitated instead.
Neutralization and precipitation
Correct. A toxin is soluble, so antibodies neutralize its action and cross-link toxin molecules into precipitating complexes; viruses are neutralized and agglutinated, bacteria opsonized.
C.cite: Immunity_Lecture_Recorded.pptx, Slides 54, 58

C.topic: Anemia by cell size and marrow response
C.io: Discuss the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of red blood cell disorders
C.q: Which anemia is listed in the microcytic group?
opts: Sideroblastic anemia
Correct. The microcytic group (mean cell volume below 80 fL, femtoliters) lists iron deficiency, thalassemia, inflammation in some cases, and sideroblastic anemia.
Megaloblastic anemia
Megaloblastic anemia, from vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, is MACROCYTIC (above 100 fL). Sideroblastic anemia is the microcytic one here.
Anemia of marrow failure
Marrow failure or infiltration is listed under the NORMOCYTIC anemias (80 to 100 fL). Sideroblastic anemia is the microcytic one here.
Anemia of renal disease
Inflammation or renal disease is listed under the normocytic anemias. Sideroblastic anemia belongs to the microcytic group with iron deficiency and thalassemia.
C.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 33

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of pericarditidies
C.q: A serosanguinous pericardial effusion is secondary to which causes?
opts: Heart failure and hypoproteinemia together
These produce a serous transudate rather than a serosanguinous effusion.
Obstruction to lymphatic drainage alone
Lymphatic obstruction produces a chylous effusion. The serosanguinous type follows blunt trauma, surgery or resuscitation.
Penetrating cardiac trauma only
Penetrating trauma produces frank blood in the sac, a hemopericardium.
Blunt trauma, cardiac surgery or resuscitation
Correct. All three involve mechanical force on the chest, which is what puts blood into what would otherwise be a serous fluid.
C.cite: 6. Cardiac Pathophysiology for posting.pptx, Slide 68

C.io: Describe the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of coagulation disorders
C.q: After initiation, which enzyme-cofactor pair activates factor X?
opts: Factor IXa with factor VIIIa
Correct. In the factor X activation step, IXa with its cofactor VIIIa activates X to Xa; Xa with Va then generates thrombin.
Factor Xa with factor Va
Xa with its cofactor Va acts one step later: it converts prothrombin (II) to thrombin (IIa). Factor X is activated by IXa with VIIIa.
Thrombin with factor XIIIa
Thrombin and XIIIa act at the end: thrombin turns fibrinogen into fibrin and XIIIa crosslinks it. Factor X is activated by IXa with VIIIa.
Plasmin with protein S
Plasmin degrades fibrin in fibrinolysis, and protein S helps activated protein C limit coagulation. Factor X is activated by IXa with VIIIa.
C.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slides 43, 44

C.io: Review the anatomy of the vascular system
C.q: Which tissues have the highest density of capillaries?
opts: Skin and subcutaneous fat
Both have comparatively low metabolic rates and correspondingly lower capillary density.
Myocardium and brain
Correct, because capillary density tracks metabolic rate — tissues that consume the most oxygen need the shortest diffusion distances to reach it.
Tendon and ligament
Dense connective tissue such as tendon and ligament is relatively poorly vascularized and has a low metabolic rate.
Cartilage
Cartilage is avascular, at the opposite extreme from the tissues named.
C.cite: SV Vascular Pathophys I Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 11

C.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of vascular pathologies
C.q: Which vasculitis is classified as large vessel?
opts: Polyarteritis nodosa
Polyarteritis nodosa is classified as medium vessel, alongside Kawasaki disease.
Kawasaki disease
That is classified as medium vessel alongside polyarteritis nodosa.
Systemic lupus erythematosus
Systemic lupus erythematosus falls under the small vessel immune complex subgroup rather than large vessel.
Giant cell arteritis
Correct. Polyarteritis nodosa and Kawasaki disease are medium vessel, and the small vessel group splits into ANCA-associated and immune complex subgroups.
C.cite: SV Vascular Pathophys I Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 32

C.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of vascular pathologies
C.q: What two quantities determine blood pressure?
opts: Vascular resistance and cardiac output
Correct. Resistance is regulated at the arterioles by neural and hormonal input; output is heart rate times stroke volume, with stroke volume influenced by blood volume.
Blood viscosity and vessel length
Both influence flow in principle, but the two determinants named are resistance and cardiac output.
Heart rate and respiratory rate
Heart rate contributes through cardiac output, but respiratory rate is not one of the determinants.
Hemoglobin concentration and oxygen saturation
Hemoglobin concentration and oxygen saturation determine oxygen carriage rather than arterial pressure.
C.cite: SV Vascular Pathophys I Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 19

C.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms involved in immune processes
C.q: Which step follows adherence of the microbe to the phagocyte?
opts: Pseudopods engulf the particle
Correct. The sequence is: the microbe adheres; pseudopods engulf it into a phagosome; the phagosome fuses with a lysosome; enzymes digest it; residual material leaves by exocytosis.
Lysosome fuses with the vesicle
Fusion with a lysosome comes after engulfment, once a phagosome has formed.
Residual material is exocytosed
Exocytosis of indigestible residue is the final step, after digestion in the phagolysosome.
Acid hydrolases digest the microbe
Digestion by lysosomal acid hydrolases happens later, inside the phagolysosome.
C.cite: Immunity_Lecture_Recorded.pptx, Slide 26

C.io: Discuss the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of red blood cell disorders
C.q: What is extravascular hemolysis?
opts: Red-cell rupture within the circulation
Destruction within the circulation is the other route, intravascular hemolysis. Extravascular hemolysis is premature destruction inside phagocytes.
Premature red-cell destruction within phagocytes

Correct. In the majority of hemolytic anemias the premature destruction of red cells occurs within phagocytes, the same cells that normally remove old red cells; this is called extravascular hemolysis.
Red-cell loss from bleeding vessels
Losing red cells from the vessels is blood-loss anemia, not hemolysis. Extravascular hemolysis is premature destruction of red cells within phagocytes.
Failure of red-cell production in marrow
Failed production is anemia of diminished erythropoiesis, such as aplastic anemia. Extravascular hemolysis is a destruction mechanism: premature removal within phagocytes.
C.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slides 38, 39

C.io: Describe the process of bone marrow neoplasia
C.q: Why does a clonal result alone not establish malignancy?
opts: Clonal cells carry many different rearrangements
A clonal lymphoid population shares ONE dominant receptor-gene rearrangement; that is what the test detects. The limit is that reactive or premalignant populations can be clonal too.
PCR cannot detect receptor-gene rearrangements
PCR (polymerase chain reaction) CAN determine whether a dominant receptor-gene rearrangement is present. The limit is that reactive or premalignant populations can also be clonal.
Malignant lymphoid cells are usually polyclonal
Lymphoid malignancies often share a dominant receptor-gene rearrangement, so they are clonal, not polyclonal. The limit is that reactive or premalignant populations can be clonal as well.
Reactive or premalignant cells can also be clonal

Correct. A clone is a population descended from a common progenitor, and reactive or premalignant populations can also be clonal. The result must be interpreted with morphology, immunophenotype and clinical findings.
C.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slides 16, 17

C.io: Compare and contrast primary and secondary immunodeficiency including the genetic basis
C.q: Why is severe combined immunodeficiency called combined?
opts: It combines primary and secondary causes
It is a primary immunodeficiency; secondary causes are acquired from disease, medications, malignancy or nutrition.
It affects both complement and antibody
The combination is cellular and humoral: profound T-cell dysfunction plus impaired B-cell immunity.
T-cell and B-cell immunity both fail
Correct. Severe combined immunodeficiency is profound T-cell dysfunction with impaired B-cell immunity; it may present in early infancy or be found by newborn screening.
It joins allergy with immune deficiency
Allergy is type I hypersensitivity; this disorder is a combined T-cell and B-cell deficiency.
C.cite: Immunity_Lecture_Recorded.pptx, Slide 76

C.io: Describe the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of coagulation disorders
C.q: What does the PT (prothrombin time) assess?
opts: Extrinsic factor VII and the common factors

Correct. The PT (prothrombin time) assesses the extrinsic factor (VII) and the common factors (X, V, II and I); the aPTT (activated partial thromboplastin time) assesses the intrinsic factors XII, XI, IX and VIII plus the common ones.
Intrinsic factors XII, XI, IX and VIII
The intrinsic factors are assessed by the aPTT (activated partial thromboplastin time), not the PT. The PT assesses extrinsic factor VII and the common factors.
Plasmin's breakdown of fibrin
Plasminogen becoming plasmin to degrade fibrin is fibrinolysis, a separate process. The PT assesses extrinsic factor VII and the common factors.
Platelet adhesion via von Willebrand factor
Platelet adhesion is a platelet function that von Willebrand factor supports. The PT assesses the coagulation factors: extrinsic VII and the common factors.
C.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 44

C.io: Review the anatomy of the pulmonary system
C.q: Across how many thin layers of the respiratory membrane do oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse?
opts: Two
Too few. The respiratory membrane has six thin layers, from the alveolar fluid with surfactant to the capillary endothelium.
Four
Too few. Oxygen and carbon dioxide cross six thin layers, including two basement membranes and the interstitial space.
Six

Correct. Oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse across six thin layers: alveolar fluid with surfactant, alveolar epithelium, its basement membrane, the interstitial space, the capillary basement membrane and the capillary endothelium.
Eight
Too many. The respiratory membrane is six thin layers between alveolar air and the red blood cell.
C.cite: 9. Pulmonary Pathophysiology - Ward 2026 (rebuilt from recording).pptx, Slide 4

C.io: Describe the effect of aging on the immune system
C.q: How do changes in older adults affect immune responses?
opts: Weaker responses to new antigens
Correct. In older adults, changes in lymphocyte function and repertoire can reduce responses to new antigens, and autoantibodies become more common.
Stronger responses to new antigens
That reverses it: lymphocyte changes with age reduce responses to new antigens.
Disappearance of autoantibodies
Autoantibodies become MORE common with age; clinical findings determine their significance.
Return of maternal IgG protection
Maternal IgG protects neonates and declines in infancy; it has no role in old age.
C.cite: Immunity_Lecture_Recorded.pptx, Slide 77

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of different pulmonary diseases, including: Acute respiratory failure
C.q: Which category of acute respiratory failure shows hypoxemia with a normal or low carbon dioxide?
opts: Hypercarbic ventilatory failure
Ventilatory failure is insufficient removal of carbon dioxide, so carbon dioxide rises (hypercapnia).
Hypoxic respiratory failure
Correct. Failure of respiration or oxygenation gives hypoxemia with normal or lower carbon dioxide: hypoxic respiratory failure.
Combined respiratory and ventilatory failure
The combined category has both problems, so carbon dioxide would not stay normal or low.
Acute respiratory distress syndrome
Acute respiratory distress syndrome is one parenchymal CAUSE of failure, not one of the three categories.
C.cite: 9. Pulmonary Pathophysiology - Ward 2026 (rebuilt from recording).pptx, Slide 8

C.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of vascular pathologies
C.q: What are esophageal varices related to?
opts: Cirrhosis and portal venous hypertension
Correct — dilated submucosal distal esophageal veins. Hemorrhoids are the equivalent process at the anorectal junction.
Valve insufficiency in the lower extremities
That produces the classic lower limb varicose veins rather than esophageal varices.
Deep vein thrombosis of the femoral vein
Deep vein thrombosis is a separate entity from varicosity, arising from the Virchow triad instead.
Atherosclerosis of the celiac artery
The mechanism is venous hypertension from cirrhosis rather than arterial disease.
C.cite: SV Vascular Pathophys I Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 36

C.io: Describe the pathological processes and risk factors for the formation of coronary atherosclerosis and plaque
C.q: At what degree of occlusion is blood flow described as compromised?
opts: Twenty-five percent
Flow is not described as compromised at this degree of narrowing.
Fifty percent
Fifty percent is the figure given for hemodynamic effect in valvular stenosis, not for coronary occlusion.
Seventy-five percent
Correct. It takes a great deal of narrowing before flow suffers, which is why plaques grow silently for years.
Ninety-five percent
Flow is described as compromised well before this, at about seventy-five percent occlusion.
