C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of different pulmonary diseases, including: Restrictive pulmonary diseases
C.q: What links each obstructive event to cardiac and cerebrovascular disturbance?
opts: Asphyxia with sudden autonomic arousal
Correct. With each obstruction, progressive asphyxia (lack of oxygen, excess carbon dioxide) and sudden autonomic and behavioral arousal result in acute cardiac and cerebrovascular disturbances.
Immune complexes in vessel walls
Immune complex deposition is a type III mechanism, not the sleep apnea pathway.
Emboli from the pharynx
No emboli arise; arousal-driven autonomic stress links obstruction to the heart and brain.
Steady hyperventilation through the night
Ventilation repeatedly fails, causing asphyxia; arousals then connect it to autonomic stress.
C.cite: 9. Pulmonary Pathophysiology - Ward 2026 (rebuilt from recording).pptx, Slides 102, 103

C.io: Review the functions of the components of the vascular system
C.q: What do the capillaries exchange?
opts: Oxygen alone
The exchange is far broader than a single substance, covering fluid, nutrients, electrolytes, hormones and waste products between blood and tissues.
Fluid, nutrients, electrolytes and wastes

Correct. Capillaries exchange fluid, nutrients, electrolytes, hormones and waste products between blood and tissues, in both directions. Their thin walls and slow flow favor this exchange of diffusible substances.
Blood cells into the interstitium
Cells are not the exchanged material; diffusible substances are.
Nothing — capillaries simply conduct blood
Exchange is precisely what defines the capillary segment; conduction is what the arteries and veins do.
C.cite: SV Vascular Pathophys I Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 8

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of different pulmonary diseases, including: Restrictive pulmonary diseases
C.q: Antibodies formed against inhaled organic particles in hypersensitivity pneumonitis produce which hypersensitivity type?
opts: Type I
Type I is IgE fixed on mast cells; here the antibodies form complexes with the inhaled particles that deposit in the lung.
Type II
Type II is antibody against antigens on cells or tissue; here antibody-particle complexes deposit in the lung.
Type III
Correct. Antibodies produced to inhaled organic particles cause a type III reaction: antigen-antibody complexes deposit in the lung, initiating inflammation and granulomas.
Type IV
Type IV is mediated by sensitized T cells, not by antibodies; antibody-antigen complexes depositing in tissue are type III.
C.cite: 9. Pulmonary Pathophysiology - Ward 2026 (rebuilt from recording).pptx, Slide 79

C.io: Describe the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of myeloproliferative syndromes
C.q: On the myeloid branch, which neoplasm arises from the red-cell line?
opts: Polycythemia vera
Correct. In the division of hematologic neoplasms by lineage, the red-cell line of the myeloid stem cell gives polycythemia vera and erythroid leukemia.
Essential thrombocythemia
Essential thrombocythemia (and megakaryocytic leukemia) arises from the megakaryocyte line. Polycythemia vera arises from the red-cell line.
Chronic lymphocytic leukemia
Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is on the lymphoid branch, a mature B-cell neoplasm. On the myeloid branch, the red-cell line gives polycythemia vera.
Monocytic leukemia
Monocytic leukemia arises from the monocyte line of the myeloid branch. The red-cell line gives polycythemia vera and erythroid leukemia.
C.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 26

C.io: Discuss the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of red blood cell disorders
C.q: Macrocytic anemias often stem from abnormalities that impair what?
opts: Hemoglobin synthesis
Disorders of hemoglobin synthesis give the MICROCYTIC hypochromic anemias. Large cells point instead to impaired maturation of erythroid precursors in the marrow.
Red-cell survival in the blood
Shortened survival defines hemolytic anemia, a destruction mechanism. Macrocytic anemias usually reflect impaired maturation of erythroid precursors in the marrow.
Plasma volume regulation
Plasma volume changes shift concentrations (as in relative erythrocytosis) without changing cell size. Macrocytosis reflects impaired maturation of erythroid precursors.
Erythroid precursor maturation
Correct. Macrocytic anemias often stem from abnormalities that impair the maturation of erythroid precursors in the bone marrow, as in the megaloblastic anemias of vitamin B12 or folate deficiency.
C.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slides 32, 33

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of acute coronary syndrome
C.q: Where are nearly all myocardial infarcts located, and which artery is most often responsible?
opts: The left ventricular walls, most often the left anterior descending
Correct. The left ventricle does the pressure work, so it is the chamber whose supply matters most, and one artery accounts for the largest share.
The right ventricle, most often the right coronary artery
Nearly all infarcts are in the left ventricular walls, and the left anterior descending accounts for the largest share.
The atria, most often the circumflex
The infarcts described are ventricular rather than atrial, and the left anterior descending supplies the largest share.
The interventricular septum only, most often the circumflex
The left anterior descending accounts for the largest share, and the infarcts are not confined to the septum.
C.cite: 6. Cardiac Pathophysiology for posting.pptx, Slide 40

C.io: Describe the pathological processes and risk factors for the formation of coronary atherosclerosis and plaque
C.q: What initiates atherosclerotic plaque formation?
opts: Deposition of calcium on the intimal surface
Calcification is a feature of established disease rather than the initiating event.
Rupture of the vasa vasorum within the arterial wall
Hemorrhage from those capillaries contributes to plaque rupture later, not to initiation.
Platelet aggregation on an intact endothelium
Platelet aggregation follows exposure of subendothelial proteins, which requires the endothelium to be damaged first.
Injury to the endothelial cells of the vessel
Correct. Everything that follows -- permeability, leukocytes, oxidized lipid, foam cells -- is downstream of that first injury.
C.cite: 6. Cardiac Pathophysiology for posting.pptx, Slide 14

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of different pulmonary diseases, including: Asthma
C.q: What mediates the immediate phase of allergic (extrinsic) asthma?
opts: Sensitized T cells
Sensitized T cells drive delayed (type IV) reactions, not the immediate phase.
Complement membrane pores
Complement pores lyse cells; the immediate asthmatic phase is mast-cell mediator release.
IgE on mast cells
Correct. The immediate phase is mediated by IgE to specific antigens; IgE binds mast cells, which release chemical mediators when the antigen arrives.
Neutrophil proteases
Proteolytic enzymes from neutrophils and macrophages destroy alveoli in emphysema.
C.cite: 9. Pulmonary Pathophysiology - Ward 2026 (rebuilt from recording).pptx, Slide 39

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of different pulmonary diseases, including: Obstructive pulmonary diseases
C.q: What is the basic lesion of bronchiectasis?
opts: Alveolar destruction without fibrosis
Alveolar destruction without fibrosis is emphysema; bronchiectasis destroys the bronchial walls.
Reversible smooth muscle spasm
Reversible spasm with airway inflammation is asthma; bronchiectasis is fixed wall destruction.
Wall destruction that dilates the bronchi
Correct. In bronchiectasis destruction of the bronchial walls results in dilation of the bronchi: an obstructive, suppurative disorder.
Gland hypertrophy narrowing the lumen
Gland and goblet cell hypertrophy with wall thickening is chronic bronchitis.
C.cite: 9. Pulmonary Pathophysiology - Ward 2026 (rebuilt from recording).pptx, Slide 60

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of different pulmonary diseases, including: Pulmonary edema
C.q: Why is the pulmonary edema of acute respiratory distress syndrome called noncardiogenic?
opts: It comes from left atrial pressure
Raised left atrial pressure is the cardiac route (mitral disease, left ventricular failure).
It comes from low plasma oncotic pressure
Low oncotic pressure (hypoalbuminemia, nephrotic syndrome) makes transudates; this edema is protein-rich.
It comes from leaky capillaries
Correct. Injury to the alveolar-capillary membrane increases vascular permeability, flooding the alveoli with protein-rich fluid: noncardiogenic pulmonary edema from leaky capillaries.
It is a low-protein transudate
The fluid is protein-rich, from leaky capillaries, not a low-protein transudate.
C.cite: 9. Pulmonary Pathophysiology - Ward 2026 (rebuilt from recording).pptx, Slides 84, 85

C.io: Compare and contrast the morphology of the various types of antibodies
C.q: What forms the antigen-binding site of an antibody?
opts: The light-chain constant region alone
The light-chain constant region sits in the arm but does not form the binding site.
Heavy and light variable regions together
Correct. Heavy- and light-chain variable regions jointly form the antigen-binding site at the tip of each arm.
The heavy-chain constant region
The heavy-chain constant region determines class and, in the Fc, effector functions.
The hinge region
The hinge lies where the arms meet the stem; binding happens at the variable regions at the arm tips.
C.cite: Immunity_Lecture_Recorded.pptx, Slides 39, 41, 42

C.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of vascular pathologies
C.q: What recruits smooth muscle cells into the developing lesion?
opts: Direct contact with circulating low-density lipoprotein
Lipoprotein accumulates in the wall, but the recruitment signal named comes from platelets and macrophages.
Factors released from activated platelets and macrophages
Correct, and once recruited they proliferate, produce extracellular matrix, and T cells are drawn in — the lesion becomes self-sustaining.
Mechanical stretch from the pulse pressure alone
The recruitment described is chemical rather than purely mechanical.
Complement deposition on the endothelium
Complement is not named in this sequence; the recruiting signals come from platelets and macrophages.
C.cite: SV Vascular Pathophys I Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 25

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of pericarditidies
C.q: What is the mechanism of cardiac tamponade?
opts: Fibrous encasement of the heart developing over years
That describes constrictive pericarditis rather than tamponade.
Adhesion of the heart to surrounding mediastinal structures
That describes adhesive mediastinopericarditis. Tamponade is external compression by fluid, impairing filling.
External compression of the chambers by pericardial fluid
Correct. The heart is prevented from filling from outside, so the muscle and valves may be entirely normal while the output collapses. Impairing filling.
Failure of the ventricle to contract because of inflammation
The impairment is of filling rather than of contraction: the chambers are compressed from outside by the fluid.
C.cite: 6. Cardiac Pathophysiology for posting.pptx, Slide 69

D.io: Describe the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of myelodysplastic syndromes
D.q: Which bone marrow neoplasm is defined by ineffective hematopoiesis with cytopenias and dysplasia?
opts: Myelodysplastic neoplasm

Correct. Myelodysplastic neoplasms (the World Health Organization's term; myelodysplastic syndromes remains in use elsewhere) show ineffective hematopoiesis with cytopenias and dysplasia, and they can progress to acute myeloid leukemia.
Myeloproliferative neoplasm

Myeloproliferative neoplasms are clonal PROLIFERATION of myeloid cells: chronic myeloid leukemia, polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia and primary myelofibrosis. Ineffective hematopoiesis with dysplasia defines the myelodysplastic neoplasms.
Acute myeloid leukemia

Acute myeloid leukemia is a myeloid malignancy with impaired differentiation and abnormal blast proliferation, distinct from the dysplastic process. Ineffective hematopoiesis with cytopenias and dysplasia is the myelodysplastic neoplasm.
Plasma-cell myeloma
Myeloma is a clonal plasma-cell malignancy of the B lineage, not a myeloid neoplasm. Ineffective hematopoiesis with cytopenias and dysplasia defines the myelodysplastic neoplasms.
D.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 18

D.io: Review the functions of the components of the vascular system
D.q: What characterizes the arteries?
opts: Low pressure, thin walls, and a role as a blood reservoir
That describes the veins, which hold the reserve volume rather than delivering at pressure.
High pressure, strong walls, high flow velocity
Correct, and the contrast with veins is instructive: veins are low pressure with thin walls and serve as the major reservoir of extra blood.
Control conduits releasing blood into the capillaries
That is the arterioles, the regulating segment rather than the conducting one.
Collection of blood from capillaries into larger vessels
Collecting blood emerging from the capillaries describes the venules, which coalesce gradually into larger veins.
D.cite: SV Vascular Pathophys I Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 8

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of different pulmonary diseases, including: Restrictive pulmonary diseases
D.q: What forms the hyaline membranes of acute respiratory distress syndrome?
opts: Inflammatory deposition of proteins
Correct. In acute respiratory distress syndrome, hyaline membranes are associated with inflammatory deposition of proteins.
Collagen from proliferating fibroblasts
Fibroblast collagen describes the fibrosis stage of diffuse interstitial lung disease.
Calcified immune complexes
Immune complexes deposit in hypersensitivity pneumonitis; hyaline membranes are protein deposits.
Inhaled inorganic dust
Inorganic dust causes pneumoconiosis; hyaline membranes are deposited inflammatory proteins.
D.cite: 9. Pulmonary Pathophysiology - Ward 2026 (rebuilt from recording).pptx, Slide 85

D.io: Describe the pathological processes and risk factors for the formation of coronary atherosclerosis and plaque
D.q: Which are listed as PROBABLE rather than major risk factors?
opts: Male sex, homocysteine and high sensitivity C reactive protein

Correct. Male sex, homocysteine and high sensitivity C reactive protein are the probable risk factors, a separate category from the major ones: age, family history, abnormal lipids, cigarette smoking, hypertension, diabetes mellitus and obesity.
Hypertension, diabetes and obesity
All three are in the major category. The probable ones are male sex, homocysteine and high sensitivity C reactive protein.
Age and family history
Both are major risk factors, listed alongside abnormal lipids, smoking, hypertension, diabetes and obesity. The probable list is male sex, homocysteine and high sensitivity C reactive protein.
Abnormal lipids and cigarette smoking
Both are major risk factors. The probable ones are male sex, homocysteine and high sensitivity C reactive protein.
D.cite: 6. Cardiac Pathophysiology for posting.pptx, Slide 10

D.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of vascular pathologies
D.q: Which conditions predispose to aortic aneurysm?
opts: Varicose veins and hemorrhoids
Both are venous varicosities from high intraluminal pressure rather than arterial risk factors.
Raynaud phenomenon and cold exposure
Raynaud phenomenon is an exaggerated vasoconstrictive response without structural wall failure.
Atherosclerosis, hypertension and smoking

Correct. Atherosclerosis, hypertension and smoking are the predisposing conditions for aortic aneurysm, a localized abnormal dilation that follows compromise in the structure or function of the wall's connective tissue.
Thrombocytosis and dehydration
Those raise blood viscosity and are deep vein thrombosis risk factors.
D.cite: SV Vascular Pathophys I Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 28

D.io: Compare and contrast the functions of the various types of antibodies and the various mechanisms by which antibodies destroy antigens
D.q: Which antibody fragment carries the effector functions?
opts: Fc
Correct. Fc contains the heavy-chain constant regions involved in effector functions; the complement-binding site lies on its CH2 domain.
Fab
Fab contains the antigen-binding regions and adjacent constant domains, not the effector region.
Light-chain variable region
The light-chain variable region helps form the antigen-binding site, which is binding, not effector function.
Hinge region
The hinge joins the arms to the stem; the effector functions sit in the Fc.
D.cite: Immunity_Lecture_Recorded.pptx, Slides 41, 42

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of pericarditidies
D.q: What produces adhesive mediastinopericarditis?
opts: Fluid accumulating without inflammation
That describes a non-inflammatory pericardial effusion, a simple collection of fluid in the sac. The adhesive form follows suppurative or caseous pericarditis, or surgery.
A dense, non-elastic sac encasing the heart
That describes constrictive pericarditis. In the adhesive form the sac is destroyed and the heart adheres to surrounding structures.
Immune cross-reactivity after streptococcal infection
That mechanism belongs to rheumatic heart disease. The adhesive form follows suppurative or caseous pericarditis, or surgery.
Suppurative or caseous pericarditis
Correct. The cardiac workload rises because the heart is now working against the structures it is stuck to. Or surgery, destroying the sac so the heart adheres to surrounding structures.

D.io: Discuss the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of red blood cell disorders
D.q: Under the World Health Organization 2024 cutoffs (ages 15 to 65), below what hemoglobin is a nonpregnant woman anemic?
opts: 10 g/dL
Too low. The World Health Organization 2024 cutoff for nonpregnant women aged 15 to 65 is a hemoglobin below 12 g/dL.
11 g/dL
Too low. The World Health Organization 2024 cutoff for nonpregnant women aged 15 to 65 is below 12 g/dL.
12 g/dL
Correct. The World Health Organization 2024 cutoffs for ages 15 to 65 are a hemoglobin below 13 g/dL in men and below 12 g/dL in nonpregnant women.
13 g/dL
Below 13 g/dL is the World Health Organization 2024 cutoff for MEN aged 15 to 65. For nonpregnant women it is below 12 g/dL.
D.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 35

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of different pulmonary diseases, including: Restrictive pulmonary diseases
D.q: Where does the airway close in obstructive sleep apnea?
opts: Small bronchioles
Narrowed bronchioles belong to the obstructive lung diseases; sleep apnea closes the pharynx.
Collapsible segments of the pharynx
Correct. Obstructive sleep apnea-hypopnea syndrome is complete or partial closure of the collapsible segments of the pharynx during sleep.
The alveolar ducts
Obstructive sleep apnea is cyclic obstruction of the upper airway; it closes the pharynx, not the alveolar ducts.
The trachea
The trachea is not the site; the closure is pharyngeal, in its collapsible segments.
D.cite: 9. Pulmonary Pathophysiology - Ward 2026 (rebuilt from recording).pptx, Slides 100, 101

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of different pulmonary diseases, including: Restrictive pulmonary diseases
D.q: What defines the restrictive lung diseases?
opts: Increased airflow resistance
Increased airflow resistance defines the OBSTRUCTIVE diseases.
Reversible airway inflammation
Reversible airway inflammation is asthma, an obstructive disease.
Decreased expansion of the lungs
Correct. Restrictive lung diseases are manifested by decreased expansion of the lungs due to alterations in the parenchyma, pleura, chest wall or neuromuscular function.
Dilation of the bronchi
Bronchial dilation is bronchiectasis, an obstructive disease.
D.cite: 9. Pulmonary Pathophysiology - Ward 2026 (rebuilt from recording).pptx, Slide 66

D.io: Compare and contrast natural and artificial immunity
D.q: Which is an example of NATURAL passive immunity?
opts: Rabies immune globulin given after exposure
Rabies and tetanus immune globulin are ARTIFICIAL passive immunity: preformed antibodies given on purpose.
Antibodies made after a natural infection
Making your own antibodies after contact with the antigen is natural ACTIVE immunity, not passive.
Maternal IgG crossing the placenta
Correct. Natural passive immunity is maternal IgG through the placenta and IgA in breast milk: preformed antibodies from another source, transferred naturally.
A vaccine series that builds antibody
A vaccine is artificial active immunity: the body makes its own response to an antigen given on purpose.
D.cite: Immunity_Lecture_Recorded.pptx, Slide 12

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of different pulmonary diseases, including: Obstructive pulmonary diseases
D.q: What produces the purulent, foul-smelling sputum of bronchiectasis?
opts: Mast cells release leukotrienes
Leukotriene release from mast cells is the immediate phase of allergic asthma.
Immune complexes fill the alveoli
Deposited immune complexes describe hypersensitivity pneumonitis.
Chyle leaks into the pleura
Chyle leaking from the thoracic duct is a chylothorax; foul sputum comes from infected bronchial pockets.
Dilated airways act as infection pockets
Correct. Bronchiolar dilatations serve as pockets of infection, producing purulent, foul-smelling sputum; Haemophilus influenzae is the most common bacterial cause.
D.cite: 9. Pulmonary Pathophysiology - Ward 2026 (rebuilt from recording).pptx, Slide 61

D.io: Describe the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of coagulation disorders
D.q: What does plasmin do?
opts: Activates factor X
Factor X is activated by tissue factor-VIIa at initiation and by IXa with VIIIa. Plasmin degrades fibrin.
Crosslinks fibrin
Crosslinking fibrin is the work of factor XIIIa, which stabilizes the clot. Plasmin does the opposite: it degrades fibrin.
Degrades fibrin
Correct. In fibrinolysis, plasminogen becomes plasmin, which degrades fibrin; this is separate from the regulation of coagulation by antithrombin and activated protein C.
Converts fibrinogen to fibrin
Thrombin (IIa) converts fibrinogen (I) to fibrin. Plasmin, formed from plasminogen, degrades fibrin.
D.cite: Pathophysiology of Blood Disorders SV Fall 2026.pptx, Slides 43, 44

D.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of vascular pathologies
D.q: What regulates vascular resistance?
opts: The capillaries, by altering their permeability
Capillaries exchange substances; they do not set systemic resistance.
The arterioles, by neural and hormonal input
Correct, and it is described as a delicate balance between vasoconstrictors and vasodilators rather than a single controlling signal.
The veins, by varying their capacitance
Venous capacitance holds the reservoir volume rather than setting arterial resistance.
The adventitia, by contracting around the vessel
The adventitia is supportive connective tissue and is not contractile.
D.cite: SV Vascular Pathophys I Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 19

D.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of pulmonary pathologies
D.q: Which mast-cell mediator in allergic asthma is the slow-reacting substance of anaphylaxis?
opts: Histamine
Histamine is listed separately from the slow-reacting substances, which are the leukotrienes.
Serotonin
Serotonin is another listed mediator, not the slow-reacting substance of anaphylaxis.
Bradykinin
Bradykinins are listed separately; the slow-reacting substances are leukotrienes.
Leukotrienes
Correct. Mast cells release histamine, slow-reacting substances of anaphylaxis (leukotrienes), prostaglandins, bradykinins, eosinophilic chemotactic factor and serotonin.
D.cite: 9. Pulmonary Pathophysiology - Ward 2026 (rebuilt from recording).pptx, Slide 39

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies and pathophysiological processes of acute coronary syndrome
D.q: How does an infarcted area change over the weeks that follow?
opts: It pales, softens, then scars by six weeks

Correct. The area becomes paler within 18 to 24 hours, then turns yellowish and soft with a border of red vascular connective tissue. Necrotic tissue is taken away by one to two weeks, and tough fibrous scar has formed by six weeks.
It is replaced by functioning muscle within two weeks
Muscle is not regenerated. Necrotic tissue is removed by one to two weeks and replaced by tough fibrous scar by six.
It calcifies within forty-eight hours
Calcification is not the described sequence. The area pales within a day, then softens, and becomes fibrous scar by six weeks.
It remains unchanged indefinitely
The area passes through a defined sequence of change ending in scar.

D.io: Review the anatomy of the blood cells
D.q: In the healthy adult, where does almost all hematopoiesis occur?
opts: Axial skeleton, proximal humerus and femur
Correct. Most hematopoiesis occurs in the bone marrow, and in the healthy adult almost all of it is in the axial skeleton plus the proximal humerus and femur.
Distal radius, tibia and the small hand bones

Wrong end of the limbs. Adult hematopoiesis occurs almost entirely in the axial skeleton and the PROXIMAL humerus and femur; the distal long bones and hand bones are not named as sites of adult blood production.
The thymus and the peripheral lymph nodes

The thymus is where T-cell precursors develop after leaving the marrow, not where blood cells are produced. Adult hematopoiesis takes place in the marrow of the axial skeleton and proximal humerus and femur.
The spleen and the liver sinusoids
Neither the spleen nor the liver is given as a site of adult blood production. Most hematopoiesis occurs in the bone marrow, almost all of it in the axial skeleton and proximal humerus and femur.

D.io: Compare and contrast the various types of immunological processes
D.q: Which of these organs belongs to the lymphatic system?
opts: Thyroid gland
The thyroid sits in the neck near the thymus but is not among the lymphatic structures labeled; the thymus is the lymphoid organ there, where T cells are processed.
Adrenal gland
The adrenal gland is not part of the lymphatic network. The lymphoid organs labeled in the abdomen are the spleen and the appendix.
Pancreas
The pancreas is not a lymphoid organ. The lymphatic system's organs are the tonsils, thymus, spleen and appendix, joined by vessels and nodes.
Thymus gland
Correct. The labeled lymphatic system includes the thymus gland together with the tonsils, spleen, appendix, lymph vessels and the lymph nodes of the neck, axilla, groin and knee.
